Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I rise to a question of privilege. I am informed by a telegram from British Columbia that the Victoria ' Times ' has reported me as having opposed in a recent debate in this House legislation for the protection of white labour in British Columbia against Asiatic labour. I desire to say that that statement is absolutely and utterly untrue.

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance in the absence of the Prime Minister whether or not there is a departmental investigation proceeding in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and whether that investigation is being carried on by the examination of witnesses under oath. The question was put the right lion, the First Minister yesterday who replied that he was unable to say. I venture to suggest that this matter is one on which the government should have some information and of which information the House should be possessed.

But I venture to make this statement, that if the western farmer was given the Canadian market for his products, possibly he would not be so averse to protection upon the manufactured goods which he has to buy. But he has a right to protest against more protection upon the goods, upon the implements which he is compelled to buy, at the same time that he has to sell his farm products at a much less price than he could get for them if he had the home market to himself. Now X have heard the statement, I think in one of the by-elections, that this government was a farmer's government. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that is about the greatest joke that has ever been sprung in this country. Take for instance the French treaty. X would be one of the first to support our French compatriots in securing a treaty with France if I was sure we would be getting some benefit in return for the privileges which we give to France. But to my mind this French treaty is a one-sided treaty, beyond any doubt. Take agricultural products, they are practically prohibited in the French market, while at the same time we have to pay a large subsidy to steamship lines, and lose about $600,000 revenue yearly. I cannot see for my part how we are going to get any advantage from this treaty.
There is another grievance that we in Ontario complain of, particularly the manufacturers, and that is that we have to pay so heavy a duty upon our coal. Our manufacturing concerns, especially in the province of Ontario, where no coal fields have been opened up, are obliged to compete with manufacturers in districts where coal is plentiful. I should like to see, in the interest of the manufacturing industries of Ontario at least, coal placed on the free list, so as to enable these manufacturers to produce cheaper than they can at the present time. Such a change would not only be in the interest of the manufacturers themselves, but it would mean that the consumer, the farmer, the labourer and the mechanic would get the articles which he required at a lower rate. Take the case of gas companies, for instance ; the gas companies of this Dominion import yearly 170,000 tons of coal annually, upon which they have to pav a duty of 53 cents per ton. In the interest ot the gas companies, to say nothing of the farmers and the manufacturing concerns, it would be an advantage if we had free coal, because it will enable them to supply the consumer with a cheaper article.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is held up to us as being a farmer himself and as having a personal knowledge Mr. CLEMENTS.
of the needs and interests of the farmers. I have nothing personal to say against the Minister of Agriculture only I think that he is deserving of censure because I do not think-that, as the minister representing the great body of agriculturists in Canada, he has not held out for their interests as he should have. I think the ministers in charge of other departments have rather outwitted him in that they have been able to get more money voted to be expended in their departments than the Minister of Agriculture has been able to secure to be expended in the interests of the farmers. Last year $5,500,000 were spent on the public works of the Dominion, whereas upon the great .agricultural class, which represents the most important interest in this Dominion, $500,000 was all that was spent. If the Minister of Agriculture would take into consideration the speech that wTas delivered by my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) the other night, it would be well for the farming community, because, if he followed the advice of my hon. friend from Dundas, he would do justice to the farmers. It will be remembered that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made the retort, during the course of my hon. friend's speech, that there was a difference between farmers, that one was a farmer and the other was an agriculturist. I would apply the term * agriculturist ' to the Minister of Agriculture, and if there is any one individual in this Dominion who has * done ' the farmers properly I believe it is the Minister of Agriculture who has so completely failed to look after their interests. The hon. member for South Wellington was in no sense justified in applying that term to my hon. friend from Dundas, because, as everyone in this House knows, my hon. friend from Dundas is an actual farmer. There is a large piping concern in the city of Guelph and I understand that the member for South Wellington has an interest in it. In this respect he has been playing the part of
*	agriculturalist ' in so far as he has been
*	doing ' the farmers of this Dominion. Lap-welded piping is largely used throughout the Dominion, especially by the farmers, and there is no lapwelded piping made in this country. Two years ago I gave expression to the belief that under these conditions lap-welded piping should come into the Canadian market free of duty so that it could be supplied to the farmers at the lowest cost. When any article is not manufactured in Canada, I care not what it is, it should come in practically duty free so that it can be given to the consumer at the very lowest cost. When any article is not manufactured in Canada, I care not what it is it should come in practically duty free, so that it can be given to the consumer at the very lowest price. When any set of manufacturers come to the Canadian government and show them that they are prepared to invest enough capital to manufacture an article in suffici-

ent quantity to supply the Canadian demand, I should always be Canadian enough to favour giving them a proper amount of protection to enable them to make a success of the industry. In the large piping concern to which I have already referred, they make nothing but butt-welded pipe, which is not suitable to the requirements of farmers and others and which will not stand the test as well as lapwelded pipe. Under these circumstances, I claim that instead of raising the duty from 17 per cent to 35 per cent, it should have been allowed to come in free until some of our manufacturers give evidence that they want to go into the manufacture of that article, and show the government that they are prepared to make it in sufficient quantity to supply the Canadian market. If the Minister of Agriculture wants to properly represent the great agricultural class, instead of adopting legislation which in many cases has been a great detriment to the farmers, he should look after their interests with respect to the questions with which they are especially concerned and see that they receive that consideration from the government to which they are entitled. Upon two occasions in this House I offered the suggestion that there should be a rigid inspection of wire fencing. Our farmers in the west, in Ontario, in Quebec, and especially in the older provinces, purchase yearly hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of wire fencing. While I believe that all the wire fencing, as far as the wire itself is concerned, is about of the same quality, I can show you in the district from which I come fencing which was purchased by farmers twenty years ago which is good fencing to-day and which has proved a good investment to the farmers who bought that fencing. I can show you hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of fencing that was bought two or three years ago which is practically useless to-day from rust, and one of the reasons for this condition is that it has not been subjected to that rigid government inspection which should be insisted upon by the Minister of Agriculture in order to protect the farmer and which has been undertaken in other instances.
The farmers are in this position simply because the manufacturers are not using the proper galvanizing for the fencing. It is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture to see that a proper inspection is made so that every rod of fencing should be stamped and the farmers in buying it would know that they were purchasing a proper article. The minister should afford such protection as this to the farmers instead of pretending to protect them as he has done, for instance, in the pork regulations. If these pork regulations had been carried out to the letter in the section from which I come, not one farmer in ten now raising pork would be raising it. When the regulations were "introduced, the pork manufacturers took advantage of them to beat down the farmers and then we have a protection against American pork of only 2 cents a pound, so that every farmer in Canada to-day, especially in the pork raising sections, has been compelled to sell his pork at a price from $1 to $1.50 a hundred less than he can possibly raise it for. There is not a farmer in Ontario to-day who, if put upon his oath, could say that he has sold 100 pounds of pork this year at a profit. I know whereof I speak, I know something of the raising of pork, I have been careful in feeding but this year had I sold the grain which I fed to swine and given the hogs away, I would have been $500 better off than I am. As I have said, the farmers are placed in this position first by the pork regulations, and second by the insufficient protection against the inroads of American pork upon this market. It should be absolutely prohibited instead of being permitted to usurp the Canadian market.
i nave protested against the policy of the government in regard to cold storage. In my section the climatic conditions are such that fruit ripens practically two weeks before it does in any other part of the Dominion, and in such a section the government could well afford to establish several large cold storage plants to demonstrate what it is possible to do by means of a proper cold storage system. Such an example would force others to go into it and that would be accomplishing something for the farmers. I believe that such a government cold storage plant could be run at a profit to the government as well as to the very great advantage of the farmers of that section of the country. Last year parliament voted $1,000,000 to assist in the establishing of cold storage throughout Canada. Thirty per cent of the cost of the plants was to be given as government aid. * n,ly sectioii no advantage has been taken ot that provision to any extent. It shows that the business men do not consider it a fair business proposition ; they do not care to invest 70 per cent of the cost and have the government control their establishment. As I have said, if the government bore the whole expense they could well afford to build several large cold storage establishments in sections of the country where they are most needed. They would be an advantage to the farmers, to the canners and to manufacturers generally. It has been reported to me that an immigrant who arrived in Canada some time ago, engaged with yon as a farm labourer. I would be pleased if you would let me know if such is the case, stating if he is still with you, what kind of satisfaction he is giving, and what wa?es he is receiving. I desire this information in order to form a fair opinion as to the satisfaction immigrants are giving to Ontario farmers. Please reply on space underneath and use inclosed envelope, upon whch no postage is required, in mailing your answer to me.
Your obedient servant,

Superintendent of Immigration.

I want to apologize for taking up so much of the time of the House, but as certain insinuations have been made in this House and as this agent and the department are shown up in connection with this matter, I propose reading some of the letters which were received by the Superintendent of Immigration from farmers in the neighbourhood of Chatham. In the tirst place, I have a letter written by Robert Gray with reference of Arthur Dungate, an immigrant who was placed with Mr. Gray. Mr. Gray says :
Fairly good man, still with us.
Underneath there is stamped upon the letter 1 claim deducted.' My reason for reading this return is that this agent placed farm labourers with manufacturers and other concerns and was therefore not entitled to the bonuses that he received. There is another letter from Mr. James Cornhill as follows :
We have seven Englishmen working for us in our brickyards here, but no one by the name of G. Head. You inquire about some of the men coming -out recently. I find them to he good workers and very sober and industrious fellows.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) JAMES CORNHILL, Frick manufacturer.
Claim deducted.
The next has reference to E. R. Leach, wife and three children.
I airly good man while with us; not here now.
(Sgd.) ROBERT GRAY.
Claim deducted.
Mr. Gray is a carriage manufacturer in the city of Chatham. There is a leter from L. English, Chatham, as follows :
Dear Sir,-We hare received several notices from you in reference to immigrants engaged with us. We only had one man, a Mr. Do-eherty, wife and four children. We engaged him 2084
at 75 cents per day, free house, wood and milk. They just stayed four days, as he said he did not care to be so far from the city, which was only two miles. I don't know why our names was sent to you. We certainly was disgusted with the one we did have. Beer seems to he the greatest trouble with these people. Pardon for not answering your other correspondence.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) LESLIE ENGLISH,
Claim deducted.
The next has reference to William Sault, wife and two children :
No good; worked a week.
(Sgd.) ROBERT GRAY.
Claim deducted. [DOT]
The next is from Robert Millinn another carriage manufacturer in the city of Chatham. It has reference to Joseph Gumbrell, wife and one child. This claim was also deducted.
Why were the claims deducted?	-

When I asked for this return the department undertook to trace up the operations of this agent and when they found that, instead of placing these people with farmers, he had placed them with manufacturers the claim for compensation was deducted.
The money has never been returned?
No, the money has never been returned.
What do you mean by ' claim deducted '?
The department have deducted these claims, but they have not received the money back from the agent. He still holds the money. He was paid for them all.
And paid for them as farm labourers ?

Yes, paid for them as farm labourers. The next -letter Is from Eliakirn Newcombe and has reference to Edward Merry and wife. The letter is as follows :
Dear Sir,-I have never heard tell of such a man as you speak of. I had one of my neighbour's boys working for me last year.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) ELIAKIM NEWCOMBE.
Claim deducted.
There is another from Thomas Anderton referring to Richard J. Paget:
Sir,-I did engage Richard J. Paget who worked for me at $12 per month for the first month and $20 for the following month if he gave me satisfaction. This man had his supper with me on Saturday night and three meals on Sunday and one more meal on Monday morning and I have never seen or heard of Mr. Paget since then, but I think he went back to Chatham. I told him as he was going if every one used him as well in Canada as I did he would be lucky. He never did anything for me not even feed a chicken.
Yours truly,

Claim deducted.
He is a farmer. Here is a letter from B. Jordan regarding Joseph Cook. He says:
Jos. Cook was a good fair man, worked live months, $10 a week. He left to work in beet fields.
Geo. Degard was a very good man, worked about three months.

Pope worked about four months. He left to work for Blight & Fielder.
F. Mumford was a very good man, worked five months, $10 a week. He left to go to work in Wallaceburg Sugar Factory.
These are all very good men.
Victor Story I did not know. He didn't work for me.
Victor Storey is reported by the agent to be with this man Jordan.
There is a letter from J. Storm regarding Alexander Martin, wife and child, on whom there would be a bonus of $6. It reads :
I wrote for a man and I didn't get one. If you sent a man and his wife, he didn't come to me. He has dropped off at some other place.
J. Jinks supposed to be a farmer, writes regarding T. Salter wife and child, on whom there would be bonuses of $0 :
Please excuse me for not answering your first notice on the grounds that I never had an immigrant and took no notice of your notice. I sent in an application last spring, also to the local agent in Chatham, J. S. Waugh. Both were for single men. So information is a little short here.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) JOHN JINKS.
There is one here from C. Terry as follows :

W. D. Scott, Esq.
Received this letter. As I am not a farmer, nor do I know of a C. Terry, either a farmer, or any other occupation, nor of a Mr. Butler.
Yours,
(Sgd.) CHARLES TERRY,
Cab driver.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have given evidence enough from this return amply to show to this House what has been going on in the Immigration Department regarding immigration agents who do not act honestly in that capacity. I do not blame the agents so very much ; I blame the system under which the government have allowed these agents to act. I say they should not have been given a free hand, as this agent was, to pay out money which belonged to the people of this country. I want to censure the Immigration Department for having paid out money in the reckless manner shown by this return, and then been compelled to ask the agent to return $600 which does not belong to him. If he were a brother of mine, I would say that this agent ought to be prosecuted.
Hasn't he been arrested yet ?

He is running at large so far as I know, and I suppose this will only be a step to his getting promotion, as a great many others of the same class have been promoted by this government in other departments. I am looking forward to this gentleman getting promotion rather than prosecution. I hope that the government will see that that money is returned, because it belongs to the people of this country, and does not belong to the government or to any agent of the government. But the government evidently do not prosecute for fraud. I suppose we might give hundreds of cases of agents who acted in the same manner as this agent has done, and who have been promoted. I do not expect that in this case the government will attempt to collect a dollar. I want to say that there are many worthy immigrants in that district. Many of those English immigrants are willing to work and to accept what they can get. and will, I believe, make good Canadian citizens so long as they get a fair show.
They were all dumped into that riding, they came there in such numbers that there was not enough work for them, and they had to be placed on the hands of the public. That is one of the greatest detriments to this Dominion, because it is only natural that such people would write home to their friends, and possibly many who would make excellent immigrants and citizens would be discouraged in coming out. That is why I say the whole system carried on by this government is wrong, and I hope the government will see fit to cancel this, bonus for the bringing of immigrants into this country. I think there is encouragement enough in the country itself to cause immigrants to flow in without this additional incentive, and I believe immigration will continue to come in without our paying out a million dollars a year in bonuses to agents for bringing it. I believe that we could even take the step which the American union has taken and get a revenue for our immigration instead of paying out a million dollars in bonuses. I have spoken in what I consider the interests of the agriculturists. I want now to look at the question from the manufacturing standpoint. It was a great mistake when this government, by their revision of the tariff, practically wiped out the woollen industry. They thus practically destroyed many millions of dollars which were invested in woollen mills. Look around this Dominion and you will only find a few woollen mills running to-day. That certainly is no credit to this government. In a few remarks I delivered in this House a year and a half ago. I pointed out that a vast amount of shoddy goods were allowed into our market under the low tariff and that these goods were a detriment to every mechanic and labourer who purchased them. Besides that importation was the cause of depriving of work thousands of mechanics

who were formerly employed in our woollen mills. That policy was thus detrimental, from every point of view, to our mechanics and labourers. In 1890, when we had a tariff sufficient to protect the industries of this country, we imported $11,000,000 worth of woollen goods on which we collected $3,157,000 in duties. But in 1904, under the low tariff, we imported $15,159,000 worth and only collected $3,953,000 revenue. In other words, inside of five years there was $5,000,000 of low class goods imported which took the place of goods manufactured by Canadian labour and we only got the same amount of revenue. And I will say this, that I believe no woollen goods were made anywhere equal in quality to the woollens manufactured in this country. It is not to the credit of this government that they undertook to wipe out that great industry which had done so much for the people, both from the manufacturing standpoint and from the standpoint of furnishing our consumers with a better quality of goods. I sincerely trust that the government will reconsider their policy in the interests of both our agriculturists and manufacturers and give us a home market for ouy agricultural products and at the same time a superior home made article for our consumers.

LOGGIE (Northumberland,N.B.) I have listened with considerable pleasure to the hon. gentleman's remarks and congratulate him on the lengthy statement he has given the House. The burden of his complaint was that the farmers are not receiving enough protection for their pork products and that the woollen industry does not enjoy a sufficiently high tariff to be placed on a stable foundation. Then he went on to cite instances in which he claimed the government have not managed the immigration carefully and prudently and have paid out money which they should not have paid. But to my mind the very fact that the government have discovered that money has been paid out wrongfully and have endeavoured to get it refunded is evidence of the care the department is taking in the management of its immigration business, and I think it has been very well established that the immigration or the bonus-ing policy of the government is : Pay your money for value received ; when the goods are delivered, the money is paid ; until they are delivered no money is paid.
The government would never have discovered that money was wrongfully paid if I had not made a protest. It was only when I protested that this government found that out.

I am glad the hon. gentleman has been such a useful member and that those in charge of the department were wide enough awake to take advantage of the information as soon as it was brought to their notice. That is all any business man can do. The hon. gentleman tells us
that a considerable quantity of pork is imported, and he has the audacity to claim that our farmers are suffering because a class of pork is imported which Canadians do not raise.
As a matter of fact, I know from personal experience, a large proportion of the pork that is imported into Canada from the United States is a class that is not produced in this country to any great extent. It is known in the trade as ' fat back ' or clear fat pork. As a matter of fact, the farmers and packers of Canada do not produce in any large quantity this class of pork and cannot supply the demand for it. Now, if this statement of mine regarding this class of pork is true, and if this pork is used largely in fishing camps and lumber camps, is it fair or reasonable that you should heavily tax the people who consume it with the expectation that some one is benefited by it who produces a lighter class of pork in Canada? We have an example of the same kind of policy in the United States. In portions of Maine there are blueberry barrens, and the people there are so given up to the idea of protection that, for the sake of these few blueberry barrens in the state of Maine, they put a duty of 70 per cent on the canned article. But does that stop the canned article, packed in Canada, from finding its way into the United States? It does not, it simply enhances the price to the consumer. If any hon. gentleman wants this verified, let him go to Messrs. H. N. Bate & Sons in this city, and ask the price of canned blueberries for the wholesale trade. He will find that they are sold at 75 cents a dozen. Then let him write to Messrs. Francis II. Leggatt & Company, of New York, and he will find that they sell the same goods at $1.15 or $1.20 a dozen. So, to protect these blueberry barrens in the state of Maine, the whole consuming public of the United States is paying this extra duty. Is it wise to increase the duty on barrelled pork as suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Clements) especially the class of pork referred to by me as being used by our fishermen and lumbermen.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Loggie) will permit me, I would like to ask a question. So far as the statement he makes regarding American pork is concerned. which pork he claims, the fishermen require, no doubt he refers to the heavy, fat salt pork.
Yes.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that in the section of the province of Ontario from which I come we produce any amount of that class of pork and we cannot get sale for It. The Minister of Agriculture accused the farmers in my district of raising too much of that class of pork, and we are compelled

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clements) does not know it all. I am interested in a corporation that uses a large quantity of that elass of pork, and I know that when we apply to the Park-Blackwell people or the William Davis people and houses of that class, they are not able to supply that class of pork. I note what the hon. gentleman says about the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Agriculture is right. That is not the class of pork that we are adapted to raise in this country. This class of hogs is raised mainly in Iowa and is fed largely on corn. The people there raise a heavier class of hogs than we do. It is unreasonable for the hon. gentleman to ask an increase of duty. The duty is already 2 cents per pound, and I suppose that if he had his way it would be 3J cents. Well, it would only mean that the fishermen and farmers who use that class of pork would have to pay that much more.

I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned that. I congratulate the government that they did not entertain any such proposition.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clements) has referred to the woollen industry. To my mind, if an industry cannot survive at a reasonable protection in a country like this, it would be better for our people to bend their energies in some other direction. With a protection-or revenue, if you like to put it that way, because all revenue tariffs afford incidental protection and industry suited to our conditions should prosper. My hon. friend from West Kent (Mr. Clements) has the audacity to tell the people of this country forsooth, that because we are not paying a higher rate of duty than 30 per cent on woollens the woollen industry cannot survive. Now, as the motion before us is one on which we can chose our subjects of discussion, I would like to say a word with regard to the fiscal and financial policy of the government. I congratulate the country and the Finance Minister upon the wonderfully prosperous condition of our finances at the present time. We find that for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1907, we expended on capital account $11,327,791. And, while we were able to do all that, we reduced the net public debt by $3,375,117. Then, again, the fiscal year that ended on March 31 last shows the very satisfactory surplus of something Mr. CLEMENTS.
like $19,000,000-not counting, of course, the special expenditure for the Transcontinental Railway, on which, during that year, we spent no less than $17,750,000. It seems to me that wiser or more statesmanlike words could not have been spoken than those of the Minister of Finance when he said that the present is a time for caution, but-a rider to that, for I think the wise man, under the circumstances would not close his ' caution '-it was a time for courage. The showing that the hon. gentleman has made has done much, perhaps more than any one thing to maintain the high financial standing that Canada enjoys to-day and has enjoyed for a number of years past.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with a few of the allegations made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). First of all, he alleged that the Liberal party were npt true to the pledges they made in 1893 at the Ottawa convention. I want to say that it was my privilege and pleasure to be present at that convention, and I know somewhat whereof I speak; and if there was one thing at that convention that impressed me more than another it was this, that in future the tariff was to be based on the revenue principle rather than the protective principle that is in most cases, perhaps not every case. I must admit that I am a little bit tinged with the idea that our friends the farmers do have a little protection to the extent of 2 cents' a pound on pork; but practically speaking, we removed from the tariff the principle of protection.
How far?

I would invite the hon. gentleman to turn to the Trade and Commerce report, page 14, and I think he will be able to follow the figures I am going to quote. He will find that the average customs duty on all imports for the decade from 1887 to 1896, the last ten years of the Conservative regime, was 19-64 per cent. Then he will find that for the following decade, from 1897 to 1906, the average rate of duty on all customs imports was 16-88. The decrease in the ten years was 2-76. During the last ten years I refer to we find that total customs imports was $1,932,262,271, which sum applied to the 2-76 shows a reduction in taxation of $53,330,438. It would be fair perhaps to deduct from this saving in taxation the amount of bounty paid during the ten years, which, according to the blue-books, amounted to $9,501,385. That sum deducted from the sum I have already mentioned, $53,330,438, makes the reduction, or the saving that my hon. friend wanted to know about, of the appreciable amount of

$43,829,053. And yet the hon. gentleman from North Toronto in addressing the House used these words:
So I say in actuality the duty for protection has not been diminished to any appreciable extent.
As a matter of fact, it is beyond dispute that we had an actual saving to the country in the ten years, in the way of duty, of money that remained in the pockets of the people, after deducting the amounts paid for bounties, a sum no less than $43,000,000. These figures are beyond dispute. The books are there, and X challenge any hon. gentleman to prove me in error. Now, Mr. Speaker, we would not have so nice a story to tell if the prediction of hon. gentlemen of the opposition came to pass, when they said that if the liberals got into power and reduced the rate of duty, our industries would be closed up, we would not have any home industries to speak of, because the reduction in duty would take place at the sacrifice of the industries. Sir, we have proved many times that that has not been the case. We can prove as a matter of fact that although we have increased our imports? we have at the same time increased our manufactures, perhaps in quite as great a ratio as our imports have increased.

While the hon. gentleman is referring to the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto, has he thought of adding the bonuses to the taxation? The bonuses that we paid on iron were paid out of revenue derived at the rate of 19-93. On the same principle you might say that all the moneys expended on public works and everything else were all paid out of revenue.

Of course that makes my argument all the stronger. X gave the hon. member for North Toronto credit for that, because he thought it was fair to deduct that. Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I had practically finished what I had to say in regard to the taxation of the country during the past decade as well as during the preceding one, and had also made a few remarks regarding the industrial condition of Canada- as we find it to-day, and I think I substantiated by figures that the home industries of this country are in a very satisfactory condition *-that they are keeping pace with the increased population of Canada, as well as the export trade of Canada. Now I wish to make a few remarks regarding the expenditures of the country during the past decade as well as during the few years preceding the same. It is well known to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House that the expenditures of this country are divided into two classes-namely, certain recurring expenditures which are charged to consolidated account, and expenditures which are not recurrent but are rather of a permanent character which are charged to capital account. In this connection I wish to refer to some remarks of the hon. ex-Minister of Finance, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). On page 5349 of ' Hansard,' referring to the expenditures made by the present administration, he said:
Some unthinking person says they have given it all hack to the people. Not at all, every dollar of that money that is put in fixed works, such as buildings and works of that kind, which return nothing to the people except use, and the money invested in hundreds of
thousands of different constructions into which the people's money is put, is effectually barred out from the currency and from the money power of the country. It is as if it were hoarded. Much employment has been given for the time being but so far as returning any value is concerned, its usefulness has absolutely ceased. It is fixed in these constructions which are of use but return nothing in a financial way to the people of the country.
I wonder at the hon. member for North Toronto making these disparaging remarks in regard to the expenditures of the country during the last ten years ; but I wonder more when I read his further remarks, as follows :
The Conservatives in their last years of office preferred to incur a debt of $31,000,000 and leave that extra. taxation which they would have had to take from the people of the country with the people who needed it, and to do with that $31,000,000 of debt, what was necessary in the way of capital expenditure to be used and to be enjoyed not only by the people of those years but by the future generations. That is the proper way of financing.
The hon. gentleman has the audacity to tell us that for ordinary small public works the proper way to finance is to go into debt. Now, let us see what the hon. gentleman did during the last .five years that he was Finance Minister of this country. The figures I give you can find in the blue-books. In 1892 we find charged to capital account $2,104,456, but in the same year he went into debt to the amount of $3,322,403; that is to say, he had not sufficient money from current account to pay the ordinary expenditure chargeable to consolidated account, but actually had to borrow money for that purpose. In 1893 he charged to capital account $3,088,317- and borrowed $549,605. In 1894 he charged to capital account $3,862.969 and borrowed $4,501,989. In 1895 he charged to capital account $3,030,490 and in that same year he added to the net debt of the country no less a sum than $6,891,897. In 1896 he charged to capital account $3,781,311 and borrowed no less a sum than $5,422,508. These figures, when added together, prove to us that the Conservative party, during the last five years of their regime, expended on capital account $15,927,743 and borrowed no less a sum than $20,688,402. That is to say they borrowed $4,761,659 more than they paid out during the entire five years on capital account. In other words they borrowed $5,000,000 to pay' for ordinary expenditure, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite have the audacity to tell us that as they expended $31,000,000 and that they thought it was a wise thing to borrow this $31,000,000. What other way had they of paying for it? They did not have the money in the treasury, they did not have it in the revenue, and they used their only recourse which was to borrow the money. And the expenditures were

small. They were not sepcial expenditures to meet which would be the proper thing to borrow.
During the last five years of the Conservative regime, we find that they expended in round numbers $16,000,000 on capital account. Now let us see what was done by the present administration in the following ten years. I find that they expended on capital account no less a sum than $89,000,000, viz., on canals, on the Canadian Pacific Railway, on debts allowed to provinces, on Dominion land, on new public works, and during the same period although they expended $89,000,000, they added only $5,000.000 to the net public debt. Compare that with the last five years of the Conservative administration when we find that they expended only $16,000,000 and borrowed $21-, 000,000 and added ter the net debt $21,000,000. Then spent $16,000,000 on capital account and $5,000,000 on ordinary consolidated account.
Carrying the comparison still further, we find that the parties in power from 1868 to 1896, twenty-nine years - twenty-five of which were under Conservative regime-expended on capital account $204,000,000 and increased the net debt of the country $182,000,000. Compare that with the capital expenditure, during the decade I have already referred to, of $89,000,000 and yet with only $5,000,000 added to the debt, whereas the other expenditure on capital account was $204,000,000 and $182,000,000 added to the net debt. It seems to me that this comparison speaks golden words for the present administration.
How does it compare with the Robinson administration?
I have no doubt it can stand the comparison.

Is not my hon. friend giving the House wrong figures? The debt of the country in 1896 was $258,000,000. At the time of confederation it was $75,500,000. When Mr. Mackenzie was in power he added $19,600,000 to the debt. Make a calculation on those figures, and you will not get $189,000,000.

That would make it practically correct. It included Mr. Mackenzie's administration. I said twenty-nine years, twenty-five of which were under Conservative regime, and I gave the figures for the whole twenty-nine years, so that they are quite correct.
$75,500,000 and $19,000,000 would make at once $96,000,000. Deduct $96,000,000 from $258,000,000 and that will not work out your result.

That works it out exactly correct. I told you that I included the $19,000,000 in the $182,000,000 which makes it exactly correct. We expended on capital account from 1897 to 1907. $84,000,000 and Mr. DOGGIE.
did not add practically one cent to the net debt. Here is the point I want hon. gentlemen particularly to note. During this period, we reduced the rate of customs duty 13-86 per cent and the per capita debt 15-7 per cent. I think that the country deserves to be congratulated on this very favourable showing to a decade to which I have refer-ed. It shows that the words of my honoured leader, which were quoted by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), have been fulfilled. These words were :
We shall be in power before long, and when in power I promise you such an era of prosperity that it will not require statisticians to prove it. You will have it in your pocket.
It seems to me that the fact that this large amount of money could have been expended on necessary public works without our adding to the debt of the country to any appreciable amount, is an evidence of this great prosperity which the right hon. the First Minister promised.
I have pointed out to you that the Conservative party, during the last five years they were in power, went in debt to the extent of 334 per cent or thereabouts more than they paid out on capital account altogether. If the expenditures which the present administration have overtaken had been overtaken by the Conservative government in the same ratio, they would have added to the debt no less a sum than $112,000,000. That is, we have expended $84,000,000 on capital account without borrowing money, and, if you add one-third to that, you get $112,000,000. So, had they made the same expenditures with the same proportion of revenue, they would have had to spend all their revenues and borrow $112,000,000 besides'. If it were necessary, as I say it was-and there has not been any question about the necessity of expenditures on capital account-to spend this large sum of money and run the country into debt to the amount of $112,000,000 besides, should we feel like going into debt for another $100,000,000 to build the Transcontinental Railway ? I think the credit of the country would not have stood as high as it does if such had been the case. But we echo the words of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) when he said that we glory in the fact that we had this money to make these expenditures without adding to the debt. Thus we are in a position to go on with this great and laudable undertaking, the building of the Transcontinental Railway. I believe that when we are spending so large a sum of money on an undertaking like the Transcontinental, the proper businesslike way is to borrow money on the credit of the country instead of endeavouring to meet so large and such an expenditure out of ordinary revenue.
Now, let me deal for a moment with the net debt. My hon. friend from Dorchester 1 (Mr. Morin) tells us that in 1896 the debt

Then we have the mounted police. We have expended $500,000 more on that service, and I am sure we can only speak in terms of laudation of the work performed by our mounted police. Then we have $3,100,000 extra expended on the militia. We know that this is a very important service. Of course, it is much more expensive because we have taken over the permanent force, and we have had to add to the expenditure some $5,000,000. We must expect to spend more money on our militia if we are to become a great country. Then we have the Post Office Department, and 1 am sure we can only speak in words of praise of the hon. gentleman who presides over that department, and of his predecessors as well. In 1906 we expended $1,300,000 more than the Conservatives did in 1896, and with what result? We find that during the interim we have reduced the postal rate about 50 per cent. We have done more than that; we have turned deficits into surpluses, and surely we can congratulate the country over the management of the Post Office Department. Then as to the Railway Department. We find that in 1906 we expended $5,000,000 more than the Conservatives did in 1896. We find that during this time the railway earnings have more than doubled. Railway earnings have increased in a greater ratio than has capital account. Not only have earnings increased more than capital account, but the mileage has increased more than capital account as well. So we find this department in a very satisfactory condition. We find that we have spent $6,000,000 on Public Works. I mean the ordinary small recurring public works ; this is $3,000,000 more than in 1906 than in 1896. And who will say that a town here and a town there with

Not only are we going ahead in the lumbering and fishing industries, but we have recently discovered that we have a country rich in minerals. In the county represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Tur-geon) there has recently been discovered one of the most valuable iron deposits perhaps in Canada.
