I wish to refer briefly to the transportation question as it affects the maritime provinces, particularly the Intercolonial. This question of transportation is a burning one all over the country. Hon. gentlemen will remember that a few years ago complaints were made that the Canadian Pacific Railway were not building branches fast enough in the west and that the farmers were obliged to haul grain twenty or thirty miles. It was considered a great hardship that it should cost 10 or 15 cents a bushel to haul grain to a station to ship it. I sympathize with these farmers; I realize that it is a hardship to be so situated. But we ought not to forget that the older provinces are enduring the very same hardship to-day. We must realize that if the Intercolonial Railway is to be a common carrier for the people of the maritime provinces, that railway owes a duty to the territory adjacent to that trunk line. It must not be forgotten that practically every branch line which serves as a feeder to the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway has been taken over by these great corporations and

made a part of the system, thus feeding the trunk line and aiding the industries situated along the branch lines. It is not possible to manage these branch lines as profitably independent of the trunk line. The Intercolonial Bailway with its trunk line between Riviere du Loup and Moncton has practically a monopoly of that whole country and it is not fair to'leave the adjacent territory without proper facilities nor is it fair to expect private corporations to build branch lines, because the branch lines could not live, the population is not sufficiently large to make them paying ventures, they would not receive a sufficient return on their short haul on freight which they would have to hand over to the Intercolonial Railway which would have the long haul. It is the duty of the government and of the people of Canada, the owners of the Intercolonial Railway, to see that the territory adjacent to the Intercolonial Railway has proper railway facilities and that the industries of that locality are not retarded because of want of transportation. Simply as an illustration, I would point out that even in my own county there is a section of country between Indian town, where the railway terminates, and Red Bank, a large and thriving village, without any railway facilities, practically without any transportation facilities whatever We are trying to have a steamboat service inaugurated there but in order to do that we shall require some assistance. That section between these two places should have a railway in the interest of the country and I would ask that this matter should receive the favourable attention of the Minister of Railways and of the government. We have also a large and rich section along the Mira-michi between Newcastle and Tabusintae that deserves the consideration of the people of Canada, the owners of the trunk line of the Intercolonial Railway because they have a monopoly of transportation there and it is their duty to see that the people there do not suffer. ' They are suffering to-day because of lack of transportation facilities to enable them to send their commodities to the markets of the world on as advantageous terms as other sections of Canada. The maritime provinces are an old section and deserve the attention of the government even as much as the western provinces, and I ask on behalf of the maritime provinces, and particularly the sections I have indicated where the Intercolonial Railway is the only means of transportation, that branch lines should be constructed as a part of the Intercolonial Railway system. Where there is another railway, the situation is not so bad, as one railway will compete with another; but where there is only the one line and that owned by the government, it is the duty of the government to provide efficient transportation facilities. We in the maritime provinces never say a word about the cost of the canal system in Ontario and Quebec; that is provided in the interest of the countrv at large. The Intercolonial Rail-Mr. LOGGIE.
way is a part of the great scheme of confederation, it is a link in the chain that binds us together, and as such, if it is to perform its mission, it ought to provide for the maintenance of branch lines. As a matter of fact a portion of one branch line has been lying all winter unoperated and to-day, although there is hardly any snow on the ground, carload after carload of freight has to be teamed. Yet there is a railway there and the blockade exists simply because the railway has not the necessary equiqment. All that is required is equipment, with proper equipment there would be no trouble in keeping the rail open all winter. It is not fair and I bespeak in the interests of the maritime provinces the favourable consideration of this matter by the government.
I was deeply interested in an important subject which was referred to in the House the other day, the All-Red line, an imperial means of transportation. When the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) was speaking, f was impressed with the difficulty of dealing with the present investments, in transportation, that is to say what is to be done with the transportation interests now operating. It occurred to me that if the great ocean lines or the corporations owning the ocean lines, could combine and form one great corporation to perform this all-red service, all infringement on existing vested interests would be obviated. The question of hauling the traffic on Canadian soil would also require consideration. Possibly some arrangement might be made between the transcontinental railways so that the traffic would be handled by the Intercolonial Railway between Halifax and the nearest point on a transcontinental railway. The Intercolonial Railway, I presume, would be double-tracked between Moncton and Halifax. For instance, at Moncton they would hand over to the Grand Trunk Pacific its share of the traffic; at St. John they would hand over to the Canadian Pacific Railway its share, and they would hand over to the Canadian Northern its share wherever its nearest point would be; and if one road got more than its share according to its mileage, there might be a division made. In that way, if we could get our capitalists of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Allan line and the Dominion line to form one great corporation, we might have its financial interests largely in Canada, and thus make Canada the centre of this great project. These are matters which ran through my mind while the hon. member for Brandon was presenting his case.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to close with a word or two of congratulation to the country, particularly on the fact that we have at the head of affairs a gentleman of the statesmanlike qualities of the Prime Minister. It was his duty, as well as his pleasure, I am sure, to represent this country on a recent occasion at a conference in London. We all followed with interest his re-

marks on that occasion. Bearing them in mind, we can see him as it were with the main sheet of the ship in his hand rounding a big boulder at the entrance to the conference, while inside we see dropped in the placid waters of the conference the anchor bearing the title " Imperial Conference." We certainly should feel proud that we have at the head of this young and rising nation a gentleman of the capacity of the Prime Minister. Then we gave him a royal welcome back to his own country. He is not long back, however, when we hear a flurry out on the western coast-the Japanese are overflowing our country! Listen to the prudent words of the leader of this young nation when he says : ' Patience; we must respect treaty rights ; the rights of the western provinces will be conserved, but we must not jeopardize the interests of our country as a whole.'. I do not quote the exact words, but they were words to that effect; and we know what a happy issue they had. To-day we have practically what the Prime Minister said would come- the rights of the Pacific province have been conserved and yet the integrity of the treaty has been maintained. Then we find him at the neighbouring industrial center of Canada, Toronto, and what does he say there of the proposed All-Bed line? He said he would not dictate to the mother of parliaments, perhaps that would not be becoming but he would remind the Imperial authorities that they had subsidized a service, very much like the proposed fast Atlantic service, from the motherland to a foreign port, and perhaps it would not be too much to ask them to do the same for their own kith and kin. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that these were the words of a statesman, and we all congratulate ourselves and the country at large that at the head of the affairs of this young and thriving country we have an hon. gentleman who can thus wisely guide the ship of state, so that we realize in our own pockets the fulfilment of what he said down in Halifax, as quoted by the hon. member for North Toronto. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen, for the attention given to me in my first attempt to say a word on the financial conditions of the country.

Mr. Speaker, in rising on this occasion I must express my reluctance, at this late hour of the night, and at this late stage of this very important debate, at trespassing on the time of the House. I would not have done so had it not been that I do not speak very often in the House; and that on this occasion it behooves those who take an interest in the welfare of their country, and I think we all on' both sides of the House do that, to have something to say at this, as we may call it, stock-taking time 209
for the Dominion of Canada. I would preface my remarks by complimenting, as others have done, the Finance Minister on the splendid statement he has been able to present to this House and this country in his annual budget. When we consider that this country has been eleven years under the present tariff with very little change, and when we consider the success that has been achieved by this country under it, we are led to inquire what are the special features of that tariff, as inaugurated by the present government, and specially by the present Finance Minister. The Fielding tariff, as it is commonly called, has been a very great success. It appears to be a distinctive tariff, a tariff different from almost every other tariff in existence at the present time in constitutionally governed countries. There has been a good deal of discussion as to whether it is a protective tariff or a revenue tariff. If I were to express my honest conviction, I would say that it is part of both. Its basic principle is that of a tariff for revenue ; but incidentally it affords protection for the industries of the country consistent with the requirements of the whole country. That was a plana in the platform adopted previous to the introduction of this tariff, and I think that has been lived up to. While this tariff affords a certain amount of protection, it does not decrease trade, but increases trade, and at the same time produces an abounding revenue. This seems to be a remarkable feature of this tariff. I would also refer to the preferential feature of the tariff. A preference to Great Britain had been discussed for some years previous to the introduction of this feature in the tariff, but the idea had always been that if Canada should give the mother country a preference, it would expect something in return. So when the government gave the preference to Great Britain, our friends on the opposition side found fault with them for not getting an equivalent from the British government. I might read you statements here but it would take too much time to show how public opinion stood on that matter in Great Britain at that period and also, that it has not changed since. Had the government stood on their, dignity, as members of the opposition advise, and said to Great Britain: We will give you a preference in our market when you give us one in yours, Great Britain would not have had that preference to-day. But this government conceded the preference without asking any thing in return. I claim however that the preference has been just as great to Canada from Great Britain-that is, the indirect preference, not so much the preference described in figures. There has been from the British people an indirect preference which has been of very great benefit to Canada.
In what way has it been a benefit to Canada?

In this way. It drew attention to Canada and Canada's products were asked for. Previous to 1896 many Canadian products entered the British market as American products and were sold as such in that market. Canada was to a large extent unknown in the British market on that account. But the day this preference was given, we touched the great heart of the British people, they began to inquire among themselves, what can we do for Canada which has done so much for us? In that way we gained the good will of the English people and that amounts to a great deal in the matter of trade.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to tell us whether Canadian goods are sold in the British market out of sympathy for Canada or whether it is not because of the quality of the goods?

I would answer that question in this way. At the beginning of the increase of our trade with Great Britain, it was largely due to a sentiment, but now it is due both to sentiment and quality. Through the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture very largely, the status of our products that enter into immediate consumption in Great Britain has become' so improved that they are now asked for on their merits, but the sentiment in our favour still exists and our market is extending, in consequence of that sentiment to a great extent, in other products. That is undeniable, and I am astonished that members on the other side, such as the hon. member for Lambton, should endeavour to combat that idea. The figures are there and they show that since we gave that preference, our exports began to increase and our trade to expand.
Let me now say a word on the intermediate feature introduced into our tariff. That is practically a new idea, and I notice that the Americans are studying our tariff with the idea of incorporating this very feature into it. It stands to the credit of this government that they introduced this feature, it is a tribute to their inventive genius, and by means of it they have been able to negotiate the French treaty. My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is very anxious to have the markets of the German empire opened to Canadian products. Well, if we are to obtain any advantage in that market, we will get it under the intermediate tariff.
Then why do you not get it ?

I think that events are moving in that idirectioni The Germans are gradually coming to their knees and you will soon find them ready to negotiate with this government. When we Mr. McKENZIE.
look at the revenue and find what surpluses we have to our credit, when we find that we have a surplus of $19,000,000 this year over actual outlay, that is something we ought to congratulate ourselves upon. Our post office surplus is considerably over $1,000,000, which is very gratifying. I have a quotation here from an English authority, which I shall read to the House. Commenting on our preferential tariff, Mr. Asquith said :
The United Kingdom could not adopt any form of preference involving the taxation of corn, meat or raw materials. The colonists on their part could give no form of preference which would admit the British manufacturer on level terms into competition with their own protected industries. That was the principle upon which the Canadian, the best of all colonial tariffs, was based. It was a principle still more conspicuous in the new Australian tariff. If the government left office to-morrow he would wish them to be judged as to whether they had not justified the confidence of the nation in their colonial administration. ^
That is the testimony of an eminent authority in Great Britain regarding our tariff. Let us take ten years as a comparison in the matter of imports and exports between Conservative and Liberal regime. Take the total imports of 1896, they amounted to $118,011,508. In 1897 they had risen to $359,793,278. Our total exports from Canada in 1896 were $121,013,852. In 1907 they had risen to $258,171,674. Or the total trade in 1896 was $239,025,360, and in 1907 $617.964,952. I wish to give the figures here to show the increase of our trade with Great Britaiu. Our trade with Great Britain in 1896 amounted to $99,513,758, including coin and bullion. In 1906 it amounted to $202,276,456, so that we have the gratifying fact that our trade with Great Britain increased $102,762,729 from 1896 to 1906.
Look at the tariff from another standpoint. The debt of Canada was $50.09 per head in 1S96. In 1906 it was reduced to $42.84 pet-head. Under Conservative rule our population in eighteen years increased 4 per cent whereas, during the last eleven years of Liberal rule it increased 25 per cent. Our foreign trade in the eighteen years of Conservative rule increased about 16 per cent, whereas in the last eleven years of Liberal rule it increased 158 per cent. The trade in 1896 was $42 per head and in 1907 $93 per head. If we turn to the rates of duty, we find that in 1889 the rate was 31-86 per $100 worth of dutiable goods imported into Canada; in 1891 it was 31-38, and in 1896 29:97, showing that under the present tariff, while the duty has been decreasing the revenue has been increasing. From 1896 there has been a gradual reduction until the rate reached the lowest point, 26-33, or a difference of 3-63 per $100 in favour of Liberal administration.
Now we come to the expenditure. And a great deal has been said by the opposi-

tion members concerning the increase of expenditure. The amount expended on capital account during eleven years of Conservative rule amounted, in round figures, to $80,000,000. Of this, as has been stated by previous speakers, the Conservative government borrowed $62,000,000-they added that much of their expenditure to the public debt. During eleven years of Liberal rule, $127,000,000 has been spent on capital account of which only $5,000,000 was borrowed. And I may say in passing that of the $127 000,000 spent on capital account by the Liberals during the last eleven years, $90,000,000 has been spent in improving the transportation facilities of the country.
Now, I am free to say that I am not in favour of extravagant expenditure either in public or in private affairs. But I realize that no private individual and no government can afford, in a young country like this, to hoard money for the sake of what it will bx'ing by hoarding. Canada is much in the position of a farmer or business man. If a man has a farm that requires improving-as many of our Canadian farms *do, and progress in this line in Canada is steady-if he has the money to improve his farm, he is foolish if he does not spend the money in the necessary improvements. A man must pay attention to his business and improve his facilities-to stand still is to go back. And the same is true of a business man engaged in a store, factory or office. A man cannot afford to stand still. He must progress, his business must grow, or others will go ahead and he will fall behind. The same is true of the country. We want economical and wise expenditure, but we do not want the affairs of the country to stand still-' progress ' must be the word. Members of the opposition have been pretty constantly talking about expenditure, and, I have no doubt, will continue to talk about it when, in the country, they speak of the actions of this government. But when they do so, I would like them to notice what members their own side propose that the government should embark in. They all have their proposals involving expenditure of- money. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) would consider the advisability of government ownership of public utilities, an idea that would involve millions upon millions for this country. My hon. friend from East Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) has an idea in the shape of free rural mail delivery, on which he has given us a great deal of information.

May I ask the hon. gentleman, is he opposed to adopting it in his riding ?
Mr. MeKENZIE. At the present time, yes. I hope that the time may come when I can say : ' No.' But that time has not 2091	*
come yet. I wish to be perfectly candid in the matter. I do not think the people of my riding would thank me for advising this government to embark upon such an extravagant expenditure as that at the present stage of our history. However desirable it might be, it would add some millions to our expenditure. Then the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. E. D. Smith) has been complaining a great deal about the Department of Agriculture. He wants more fruit inspectors, he wants better cold storage facilities. And hon. members on both sides of the House, including a large number on the opposition side, are in favour of the construction of the Georgian bay canal, which would probably cost $130,000,000. And our friends from Prince Edward Island want a tunnel. When men so strongly advocate economy of expenditure, it is rather surprising that they should even allude to such enormous expenditures as they propose to be added to what the country must spend in other directions.

We believe that these would be economies in some cases.
Mr. MeKENZIE. I am not disputing it, but it would involve a large expenditure. I hope the time will come when the Dominion can give to Prince Edward Island better means of communication than are now provided. But Prince Edward Island is not disposed to wait, they want the tunnel now. According to their view, no matter what stands, this cannot stand. I would say to hon. members of the opposition that the problem we are up against in Canada is not so much to cut down the expenditure as to make the expenditure in the right direction. There is no doubt that in Canada the transportation problem is a very expensive one and one that must be met by the government. There was a time in Canada when we were pretty well content with the Welland canal, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and other existing railway connections. But the time has come when we need improved facilities. The Welland canal is too shallow, too narrow, too roundabout. The cry is for a direct route and the proposal is made to build the Georgian bay canal. The cry is for a better railway across the continent with better grades and easier curves. This demand the government is trying to meet with the Transcontinental Railway. The time may come when we shall decide that it is necessary to build the Georgian bav canal. Canada is progressing. Canada ha's begun the development of her great west; the great north is being discovered. Canada cannot afford to stand still, and I do not believe that the people, when the matter is properly laid before them, will wish to stand still. I would advise the government to go on courageously with any wise expenditures. But let the money be spent

on a system. If the Georgian bay canal is to be built, for instance, do not touch it until we can build It with a depth of 25 feet. If we must build this canal, let us build it so as to meet the requirements of the future. Vessels are constantly getting larger and of deeper draft, and canals allowing only a shallow draft will soon be out of date. But no mistake should be made by the government in taking up new schemes. They should wait until they are ready to build the thing right, keeping in mind the future of Canada.
A good deal of criticism has been levelled at the Department of Agriculture. Being speaking of agriculture, I cannot resist the temptation to look back to the period before 1890 in the history of our farmers. I can well remember those dark days; I can well remember that times were hard for the farm-era previous to 1896. The population of Canada was leaving us by hundreds of thousands, Canada was not growing and even our natural increase was not remaining with us. No change could have been more marked than that which has t^Jten place. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Clements) this afternoon whining about the poor farmer of his county. I felt that he was not doing justice to his county. I cannot see for my part why such a whine should go up from that splendid county of Kent, and by their own member in this House. I do not- think there is another member in this House who would rise up in his place and say the same regarding his county. I am sure my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. P. Christie) would not do it, and I am sure my hon. friend from Bast Huron (Mr. Chisholm) would not do it. I do not think it was fair to the county of Kent that such a statement should be made regarding it. I know they have had their troubles in Kent. I know they have had hog disease that has injured the farming industry, and perhaps they have had some other drawbacks. But I do not think the government should be blamed for that. The Department of Agriculture has done their best for the people of Kent to help them over these difficulties, both in past years and in the present year. I do not see why so much fault should be found with the government for the condition of the farmers in Kent, if they are in that condition, but I very much doubt it.
Now I wish to refer to a remark made by one of the previous speakers, I think the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). He spoke of the fact that Canada was going back in her exports as shown by the balance of trade, and instanced butter as one of the articles which showed a falling off. Now let us look at that matter for a moment. In the ten years between 1877 and 1886, the total exports of butter were $22,706,360; in the next ten years, from 1887 to 1896, the total exports had fallen to $8,252,088, showing a decrease of $14,456,272 dur-Mr. McKENZIE.
ing Conservative rule. Now in sharp contrast to that we find that in ten years under the Liberal government from 1897 to 1906, butter exports amounted to $46,599,782. The items of bacon and hams show a like result. The total exports of bacon and hams for the ten years ending June 30, 1896, were $17,-
671,000,	as against $115,000,000 during the ten years ending June 30, 1906. The hon. member for Brantford blamed the govern-men in regard to the item of butter. We all know that Ontario had a dry season last year, that the quantity of milk fell off and consequently the production of butter. We exported largely in the early part of the year and that left us short in the latter part of the year, with the result that we had to import butter again from the British markets for our own consumption. But this was only an isolated case, and may not occur in Canada again for many a day to come. I regard the agricultural interests of Canada as so important that they should receive careful consideration from any government that may be in power. We find that at the present time there is invested in agriculture in Canada $2,200,000,000. The value of farm products exported and consumed at home was last year $450,000,000. Compare agriculture with manufactures. In 1896, the money invested in manufacture was $200,000,000. and in 1906, it was $600,000,000 a sum still far below the investment in agriculture. Therefore I think that agriculture may safely be called the basic industry of Canada at the present time, and will remain so for many years to come.
Some members of the opposition have recently criticised the Minister of Agriculture severely. I think that one hon. gentleman in particular has criticised him and given him little or no credit for having done anything in the interest of agriculture. Let me refer to one of his late acts to show what he has done for this industry. It was called to my attention recently at a meeting I attended, by the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan. We are all sorry to know that last year the west was struek by a bad frost, with the result that the grain was damaged. No sooner had the Department of Agriculture here in Ottawa learned of the damage, or supposed damage, by frost, than orders were sent at once to the Ministers of Agriculture in the west, and through them to other correspondents throughout the western provinces, to send as soon as possible samples of their grain down to the department at Ottawa that it might be tested to see to what extent damage had been done. That was done as soon as the grain was threshed and got dry enough. Mr. A. H. Clark, the chief commissioner at the head of that department at once set to work experimenting with this grain, and he found the most astonishing result that but a very small portion of the oats was fit for seed, that the vitality of that grain for seed purposes had been practically destroyed.

This information was communicated to the western provinces in a bulletin; and Mr. Motherwell told me that on his way down to Ottawa, when he came to Winnipeg, the great cry was: Have you seen A. H. Clark's bulletin? This was in everybody's mouth, the information seemed to be so incredible that people were looking at one another in blank amazement. Is it possible that the immense crop of oats in those western provinces is going to be of no use for seed? Mr. Motherwell stated at a meeting in the Normal School Hall here in Ottawa, that the work done by the department in reference to that seed grain had saved the west from a total failure in respect to oats and barley, and partly in respect to wheat. He said that the prompt action of the government in testing the seeds had saved the western provinces from a great loss. Let me tell the House that Mr. Motherwell stated that his own crop of Oats looked so well and weighed so heavy that he would have sold them without any compunction for seed oats, had he not known that from the experiments made in Ottawa their vitality was destroyed. The result, he said, was a saving of millions of dollars to the west. Now that is one thing that the Minister of Agriculture has done for this country, he did it last year. Now I would like to show what Mr. Clark says about this matter.
Prior to governmental operations in the matter of guaranteeing seed supply in unfortunate districts in western Canada, wholesale business interests were sceptical as to the ability of farmers within those districts to meet present and future payments on goods- farm implements, &c., 4c. In consequence the farmers and all retail business interests within those districts found it difficult to obtain credit on reasonable basis from wholesale merchants, from banks or lo-an companies.
The very action of the government in procuring seed grain, served as a guarantee of a crop so far as seed supply is concerned and at once restored confidence on the part of business men and financial institutions that the prospective crop output for 1908 would be equal to present and future liabilities. Then and not till then were farmers in general able to procure reasonable credit to enable them to purchase supplies of seed grain on their own account. Many farmers needed more seed grain than the governments undertook to supply-namely, 200 bushels wheat, 200 bushels oats and 100 bushels bar-ley. Many thought perhaps they could get it cheaper and were encouraged in that thought, by numerous unfavourable newspaper comments Such newspaper comments also may have induced many to take the risk of sowing their frozen grain, but the fact remains that not until action was taken by the government were they able to get the financial accommodation they needed to help themselves.
This action of the government has had a very beneficial effect and Mr. Clarke has told me, immediately on his return to Ottawa, that the information that a certain district was to be supplied with seed had
a most astonishing effect. Business men and others who had refused to give credit at once loosened up, the banks and financial institutions began to lend money, and every one took a more hopeful view of the situation.
Another matter that was criticised very severely by the hon. member for Wentworth was the action of the Department of Agriculture with reference to cold storage facilities on sea-going vessels. It was stated that a-very small quantity of goods were being shipped in cold storage as compared with the quantity that was expected to be shipped. I have a return showing the number of packages that were shipped in cold storage this year and this applies to early apples and perishable fruits such as peaches and pears. There were in all thirty-one shippers who shipped by cold storage 3,847 barrels of apples as well as 94 packages of smaller fruits. The fact has been alluded to that a quantity of fruit was sent across the equator to South Africa in cold storage and landed in good condition. That fact is likewise stated here. But we have also the fact that 12,017 packages of California fruit came through Canada, sent through the Canadian cold storage in preference to their own, and this, I think we will all admit, is a tribute to the character of the accommodation which is being furnished by the ships on the Canadian route.
Again, in regard to the Fruit Marks Act, it has been very severely criticised. I should say that this year the conditions surrounding the trade in fruit have been exceptional. Fruit in the country was not up to the average, and at the commencement of the barrelling season it was thought that apples were going to advance in price. A great many people went into the business and prices went high in the orchard. After it was known that the supply was abundant, the price was decreased and a number of dealers packed a good deal of inferior fruit with the object of trying to come out even. I have here an American opinion o the Fruit Marks Act of Canada which I will read :
Comparison of American and Canadian apples by United States Vice-Consul Albert S. Phillips, Writing with reference to American and Canadian apples in Great Britain, he says:
The Canadian government has regulated these grades as to quality and size of fruit, and if packers deviate therefrom they are liable to a fine. This government control inspires dealers with confidence, and the fact of there being only three grades simplifies the trade, making it possible for dealers to have a perfect knowledge of what they are purchasing. These conditions do not obtain, however, in the United States; on the contrary, marks run from lx to 25x, and the sizes of the boxes and barrels differ in every state, thus, according to the dealers here, rendering the trade most complicated. I have been shown large numbers of barrels (Ameri-

can apples) where the packing was very uneven, consisting of small green apples on the top and bottom, with decayed fruit in the middle. It has also been pointed out to me- and judging from the fruii l have seen on the Cardiff market I am forced to admit it- that Canadian apples receive more care in gathering and. packing than the American fruit.
Quoted from ' California Fruit Grower/ December 28, 1907.
That is American testimony to our Canadian Fruit Marks Act and its results. I do not say that the hon. member for Wentworth decried the Fruit Marks Act; he criticised it, but he did not decry it. He said it was a good Act, but that it did not go far enough, and that the government should appoint more inspectors and institute a separate branch for fruit. That is a matter of expense. I think myself from my knowledge of matters in connection with the Department of Agriculture that it would be to our advantage to have a separate branch in the Department of Agriculture devoted to the fruit interests, but it means a considerable addition to the expense of the department. I think also with the hon. member for Wentworth that it would be well to appoint more inspectors, that seems to be a necessity, and that fruit should be inspected at the point of shipment as much as possible. I think these are changes that could be beneficially made, but I would say on behalf of the department that they did make an honest endeavour to carry out the Fruit Marks Act this year. We have a return showing that last year there were 30 prosecutions under the Act whereas this year they have run to 100 already and they may run to 150.
I would like to say a word before I leave this subject in regard to the recent investigation into the tobacco industry in Canada. As chairman of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization I take an interest in this matter, and the facts justify me in saying that the Minister of Agriculture has been beforehand in this matter of the growth of tobacco in Canada. Some years ago he appointed an expert to give directions as to the cultivation of tobacco. The investigation we have just gone through before the Committee on Agriculture has shown us that there is no necessity for Canada importing tobacco. It has shown us that we can grow leaf equal to the American leaf or to the leaf imported from other foreign countries, and it has also shown us that with the changes that the Department of Inland Revenue has just made in the Act it is reasonable to believe, in fact, it is almost a certainty, that when the rehandling business is in the hands of men who have capital to provide rehandling buildings in which to properly cure the tobacco we can export tobacco very profitably to England and Belgium. If this is true, and I believe it is-
I am quite satisfied that from hearing the Mr. McKenzie.
experts who have been examined

we will add another industry to the agricultural industries of Canada. I am not a tobacco user and some one might say that I have no right to speak in this way but I feel that tobacco has come into general use to stay ; we are sending out a large amount of money for imported leaf and if we can produce it in Canada we are no worse off in the matter of the consumption of tobacco than we would be if continued to import it, but on the other hand, we will have another industry added to the industries that our farmers can engage in. These are matters that we would like to talk on, but there are other matters. Before going into them I might say a word on immigration. I had almost forgotten to say anything upon that subject. The immigration branch has been severely criticised for the conditions prevailing at the present time in the matter of immigration.
Speaking of present conditions in Canada, members of the opposition have taken advantage of the exceptional conditions to criticise the general immigration policy of the government. We hear a great deal about the adverse balance of trade in Canada. As we might expect, different views have been advanced during this discussion as to whether a country can be prosperous under an adverse balance of trade. For my part I think that it is not at all surprising that we should have an adverse balance of trade in Canada to-day. A close examination of the returns will disclose that the excess of imports is largely due to the importation of raw materials on account of the great progress Canada is making in'manufacturing and the building of great railway works, particularly the National Transcontinental Railway. We heard to-day from the hon. member for New Brunswick (Mr. Doggie) of the enormous amount spent for the importation of raw cotton, while we as farmers import a large quantity of corn, our raw material. A great quantity of settlers' effects are also imported and these things together would make up the difference between the exports and imports. My solution for the difficulty would be to pump in the immigrants. That was Kipling's solution of the Japanese problem ; I do not know whether it was as true in his case as it is in mine, hut I am satisfied that mine is correct, we should have no diminution of the stream of immigration to Canada if it is of the right class. I wish to be distinct on that point, we want the class that will go on our lands, or will go on public works presently and afterwards on the land. We cannot get too many people of this class. It is true that during the last months of last year we had an excess of immigrants, many of whom have stayed around the towns and have been a burden in a sense on some towns in Ontario. A great deal has been said about the conditions in shack-

town in Toronto. When that is mentioned it recalls to our minds the conditions previous to 1896 when all over Canada soup kitchens had to he opened to feed not immigrants but Canadian born citizens, and men and women who have been in Canada for many years. We do not find that to-day and the conditions in those cities are entirely due to this excess of immigration, in the latter months of last year, of people without means who could not get work, and this, of course, was partly due to the stringency of money which restricted the labour market. That condition could not be foreseen or avoided and naturally there was some little congestion in centres like Toronto where these people congregated. So I do not think we need be alarmed about conditions in Canada. These people are moving out of Toronto as quickly as may be to public works in progress throughout the country and will very soon be earning their own livings and will no longer be a charge on the charity of the city or province.

From 1903 down to the present time British immigration has taken the lead and every year has shown an increase while the immigration from continental Europe has shown a decrease in comparison. That fact I wish to note particularly. It is a condition which we are all very glad to see. It is true that there are many countries in northern Europe from which we welcome immigration. There are countries in the south from which we do not want it. Our Immigration Department cannot be too particular to discourage immigration from these southern countries of Europe altogether. It must be remembered that unless we prohibit these people from entering the . country, a certain number of them will come. While we can keep out a certain number it is very difficult to shut the doors against immigrants coming from Europe, and the government cannot be blamed if a certain number from southern Europe do come in ; but we would blame them if they encourage that class of immigration. Immigration from northern Europe is very desirable. If we go to the western provinces, ' into the settlements of immigrants from northern Europe, while individual members may decry that immigration and discount it as compared with the British immigration, I say that these people are filling a need that we cannot fill from British sources ; we cannot get the number of people from
the British Isles, from the older provinces of Canada or from the United States we require. We have an immense country to fill. It is true that we should fill it if possible with tiie very best class possible, and the government must exert themselves to secure immigrants from the countries 1 have indicated. I would favour particularly German immigration. I have noticed that German immigrants, no matter from what country they come, whether Germany, Russia, or any other country, if they are of German extraction and belong to the German race, are desirable settlers. They came into Ontario from the United States and from the old country as well. I have them in my county and there is no better class of farmers, no better class of citizens in the country and no class that is doing its duty to the country in the way of increasing population and wealth in a greater degree than the Germans.
Why not get into their market ?

We will get there, I will help you, friend Armstrong, if I can. It is significant that we are confronted, with no great question of policy in Canada to-day. It is remarkable, that we have got away from matters of policy altogether. The policy of this government seems to have been such a success, so much above successful criticism, that the opposition, in order to get something wherewith to influence the electors, have left the weightier matters, the matters of greatest importance, and have resorted to cries discreditable to Canada, cries of graft, graft, graft, scandal, nothing' but scandal, the government of this country not worthy of the least consideration. It is true that the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) received from the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) a little consideration. That hon. gentleman said that Providence might be seen walking with him, but certainly not with any other member of the government. That is strange language for a leading politician in Canada to utter. It is almost a slur on Providence. I wonder who gave us the success we had as disclosed at our stocktaking time in this particular budget. It was not the other fellow I am sure, we do not look for blessings from him, so I think the hon. member from North Toronto must have been very hard up for an argument when he made the statement that Providence would not be seen walking with the Minister of Finance. He was with him all the time.
Now we are forced to speak of the matter of scandal. We have heard a great deal of it for several sessions. This session we are getting a surfeit of it; but I notice that the scandals of past sessions have been getting stale, and are not now so often alluded to. There was one scandal which I had

something to do with personally, having been chairman of the committee that investigated it; that is the scandal in regard to the North Atlantic Trading Company. I am going to state as briefly as I can to the House how that appeared to me, as I sat listening to the evidence day after day. The Conservative government had been in the habit of getting immigrants from Europe by means of correspondence with booking agents, corresponding with over a hundred of them. When Mr. Sifton came into power, he saw that if he could get these people united into some sort of a company and conduct the correspondence with their representatives, it would be a great improvement. Such a company was formed, and a contract was made with it, along with an agreement that the names of the members of the company would be kept secret, otherwise they could not live in the country ; they would be ostracised and perhaps imprisoned for inducing emigration from the country. The government pledged their faith that the names would be kept secret, and in pledging their faith, they pledged the faith of the people of Canada whose representatives they were. Time went on and this investigation took place, the names of the company were called for day after day. Frequently the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) who was leading the attack, would appeal to the committee to have the matter referred to the House. I often remonstrated with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, saying,
' Why not wait until we report the whole matter to the House, and then we will discuss it fully.' But, no, he wanted to get the matter referred to the House before the investigation was ended, r thought the object was to stampede the country before the truth came out. Finally the Prime Minister sent for the names, brought them to this House in a sealed envelope, rose in his place in the House, and offered the leader of the opposition to go with him into a room and open the envelope and satisfy him who the members of that company were- that there were in it no members of the government or friends of the government, or if there were he would know it. Before the leader of the opposition could say any thing in reply, his supporters shouted ' No, no '. The leader of the government turned and said : ' If you have not enough confidence in your leader to allow him to go into a room with me and open this envelope, I would suggest that you appoint three or four of his friends to go with him, and we will appoint three or four of our friends, and we will all go together into a room and open the envelope.' That likewise was refused. What reasonable man could come to any other conclusion than that it was not the names the opposition wanted, but an attempt to stampede the country with a cry that there was nothing in. I had recently Mr McKenzie.
occasion to address a public meeting. Before the meeting a leading Conservative came to me and said : * Do you know anything about the North Atlantic Trading Company ? ' I said, ' I know a little.' He said : ' Is it true that Sir Wilfrid offered to go into a room with three or four members from each side and give the names of the members of the company ? ' I said : ' Yes, that is true.' He said, ' Will you speak of that to-night ? ' I said : ' I will if you like, but this matter is getting old ; now it is teaspoons and teacups and pemmican and other little matters that are engaging the attention of the opposition, while the North Atlantic Trading Company is relegated to the past.' ' Well,' he said, ' that is a matter I want you to bring up, because if what you say is true, it means a good many votes for your candidate.' I spoke of it and tried to show that the government was justified in keeping faith with those men, and that everything was done to enable the opposition to see the names consistent with the honour of the country.

Does the hon. gentleman think that it would be satisfactory to the representatives of the people for a few of them to get the names without being able to go into an inquiry as to who those men were, whether they were fulfilling their agreement or were capable of doing so, or using their names in many other ways, as they would be obliged to do in following out the inquiry ?	'

I know perfectly well that that is the position the hon. member for East Grey takes ; I have heard him ask the same question of other speakers. If the hon. member or any other member of the opposition had been desirous of getting at the facts of the case, they would have gone that far at least. It could have done no harm, and the fact that the Premier's offer was not acceded to showed me most clearly that it was not the names they wanted. I think the opposition in this House have some interest in the honour of this country when the word of its representatives is pledged as well as members on the other side, and they should have shown that on that .occasion. I think the people of the country will take my version of the case, as they did on the occasion I have alluded to.

When a member of this House stood up and held up what was declared to be an Act of incorporation of a company incorporated in Amsterdam, and the opposition accepted that declaration as correct, and when they found out in the inquiry that that was an absolute perjury, what would they have done in this case if they had not been able to follow up the inquiry ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What difference was it where the company was incorporated ?

Did it not make a great difference in the statement of a public man on his honour that the company was incorporated, and professing to produce the Act of incorporation, when in reality there was no such incorporation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What difference would it be whether the company was incorporated or not, for ail substantial- purposes ?
Mr. SPItOTJLE. It made this difference, that they deluded the public with the idea it was a respectable company when there was no such company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Incorporation does not create respectability.
Forgery does not create respectability. People guilty of it generally get behind the bars.
If it was such a good contract, why did the minister cancel it ?

For the simple reason that the company was not living up to the contract in regard to immigration from the northern countries of Europe. They were going to countries further south where they could get immigrants at less expense and with less effort instead of going to Scandinavia where they would have to spend more and take more trouble. Previous to that being done, I had a talk over the matter with the Minister of the Interior. He gave me this idea of it and I commend him for the course he has taken. I did so as chairman of the Colonization Committee.
There is another matter in which the public have taken a good deal of interest and that is what is called the Saskatchewan valley land deal. That transaction, which is well known to hon. members, has been characterized by the opposition as a gigantic swindle. But a short history of this transaction will show that it was nothing of the kind. We all know that Osier, Hammond & Nanton built two lines of railway, one from Calgary to Edmonton and the other from Regina to Prince Albert. The company got a grant of 1,000,000 acres of land and were given a large area from which to make their selection. They found that the land was not good enough. They selected a small portion and then wanted to throw the land back on the hands of the government. I need not go at length into the transaction but I would point this out. The company were willing to take as low as $1 an acre for the land if the government would take it off their hands and give them a money grant instead. They even went so far as to institute a suit to compel the government to take back the land and give them money in its place. While this dispute was going on, a certain American firm, Davidson & McCrea, who had just closed out a land transaction in Minnesota, heard about this block of land and came up to look over it. They heard the company's proposition, and they bought from the company 1,000,000 acres at $1.75. They brought up with them to look at this land men engaged in farming in the dry states, and who were engaged in farming on a pretty large scale. They brought up three or four of these men, and three Of these are still farming in that country. These men, after looking over the land, after testing the soil and comparing it with their own dry states, made this offer to Davidson & McCrea :	If you can get us the even
numbered sections in a certain area in this territory from the government so that we can start farms on a large scale, we will make the experiment. Davidson & McCrea were not willing to go into the matter by bringing in individual settlers because they were afraid that individual settlers might not adapt themselves to the style of farming required in that country and the experiment might prove unprofitable, so they accepted the proposition of these men. And they proposed to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) that they would like to get a certain quantity of even-numbered sections so that they might establish large farms and experiment with this land in that way. The transaction was closed for
250,000	acres of land at $1 an acre, subject to settlement conditions. These conditions were that the company would put twenty settlers on twenty even-numbered sections and twelve settlers on other sections or 32 in all on each township. Just look at the transaction from a financial standpoint.

Tlie government would have given away the land for nothing in any event, hut in-, stead they got in cash $250,000 and had 32 settlers in each township as well. Look at it from the standpoint of settlement, and you have an influx of immigration of the most desirable character. You have 32 settlers established in each township and a system of farming introduced specially adapted to that Saskatchewan valley. I have been there and in almost every part of the west and I know something of the various systems of farming adapted to the different portions of the west. With regard to the soil in the Saskatchewan valley, I can say that it requires a system of farming entirely diiferent from that required by the sections around Portage la Prairie or the Red River valley. The soil of the Saskatchewan valley is hard and solid and requires deeper ploughing and more thorough pulverization. Unless that is done, you cannot have a crop grown successfully on it. I have seen crops on the soil there, which was deeply ploughed and thoroughly pulverized, and crops growing on the soil lightly ploughed as in the country further south, and while the fix'st was a great success the latter was a complete failure. Those three men whom the company sent out there to examine the land have their farms there still. They have most beautiful farms and are growing wheat successfully. The settlers around them are following the same system of farming, a system adapted to that section, and farming there could not be made a success following auy other system. This is one of the greatest advantages derived from that transaction, namely, the fact that this particular system of farming was introduced and developed there and demonstrated to be the proper system for that country. What has been the result? There has been a flow of immigration into that Saskatchewan valley since and we have several large towns, including Saskatoon, there to-day, whereas before that transaction took place the railway was running 60 miles without a settler and 100 miles with only three settlers. And the Americans are still flowing in there. The year before last and last year a Minnesota company ran their own trains right up into that country and delivered immigrants at points right along the line every two weeks. These immigrants they had collected at Minneapolis and St. Paul and ran them right through. That is the system which the Americans have adopted and that has been applied to that country in consequence of the Saskatchewan valley land deal. And that flow of immigration is going to be large again this year, and that valley, which at one time was considered a semi-ariid region, not fit for the growing of wheat, is going to yield millions of bushels. I cannot see why any one should condemn the Saskatchewan valley land transaction from Mr. McKenzie.
any standpoint. If the men who took up that contract did make some money from the rise in values, they were entitled to it, and the country has gained a great deal more than they did, and they got considerably less prices than the property has since been sold for, because these lands are appreciating in value all the time.
^ I would like to say something about the ' Arctic ' and the ' Montcalm ' scandals, but these have been dealt with already very fully. I might just mention one matter with regard to the ' Arctic ' which has been made a great deal of. I see the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) looking at me very hard.

I am wondering what you can have to say in defence of the ' Arctic ' scandal.
Mi-. McKENZIE. I shall just make reference to one item and that is the item of pemmican. The firm of Davis & Company offered to supply pemmican at 35 cents a pound. I have taken the trouble to find out what kind of pemmicau that would be.
How much did the government pay ?

$1.25 per pound, but the pemmican that could be bought at 35 cents a pound would not last on ship board on such an expedition three months. It would not keep, whereas the pemmican taken aboard the ' Artie ' when she went on her first expedition, and for which $1.25 per pound was paid, is fit for use to-day and as good as ever. So, we see there is pemmican and pemmican. I do not deny that you can buy pemmicau at 35 cents per pound. But there is a special method adopted in making pemmican that will keep long enough for the use of these expeditions to northern latitudes and that is what was bought for the ' Arctic.' I do not see why the two sides of the case should not be given. I am surprised at the use that has been made of the affidavit in the matter of this pemmican. Had the other and cheaper pemmican been taken, the chances are that the stuff would have become so rank long before the three years' cruise was over that the men could not use it, or, if they did use it, the result would be sickness and death.
What did the affidavit say?
It was read in the House.

It stated-if the hon. gentleman will permit me-that the manager of Win. Davis Company had examined the pemmican and would agree to supply them in quantities at 35 cents per pound, what the government were paying $1.25 per pound for.

If that is the wording of the affidavit, I will accept the hon; gentleman's word for it. At the same time, I

do not believe it could be done, for X have gone into this matter to some extent. The process is so elaborate and so difficult, and the quantity is so reduced, that, taking meat at the ordinary prices and prepare it for long keeping as I have stated, the price is increased.

If the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) will permit me-I do not wish to interrupt him-I will read a portion of the affidavit:
I have examined a sample of the pemmican so-called, furnished for the ' Arctic ' expedition. and the firm with which I am connected would be pleased to furnish to the government or any institution or individual an article similar and equal in quality, in lots of 1,000 pounds or over, packed in 10-pound tins, boxed, strapped and shipped to any point in Canada, for 35 cents a pound.
This was signed by the manager of the Wm. Davies Company.

Where doctor's differ, it is hard for us to decide. The affidavit seems straight enough, but I have satisfied myself that they cannot do it at the figure. He could produce pemmican, but it would not keep for the length of time required for such an expedition. Now, I wish to say a word about transportation. A good deal has been said about the Hudson Bay Railway. Looking to the future of Canada, I must say I am very much in favour of something being done to provide a road to Hudson bay. I thiuk the country will require an outlet for the northern part of the west, not immediately perhaps, but within five or six years. I have heard a good deal and read a good deal about the northern part of Canada, and am very much of opinion that a great part of our country there is adapted for agriculture, that it has greater resources iu the way of valuable minerals and otherwise than we are now aware of. I am likewise of opinion that our northern country is improving in climate. From what I can read, the low temperature is passing away from northern Canada and is travelling eastward over Greenland and towards Siberia, and that, as years roll on, our west and northwest will grow milder in climate and we shall have a great asset for the production of agricultural products in that north country. The Hudson bay road is not a very long stretch, only 500 miles. And, seeing that lands in that part of the country have never been alienated from the government, I think it would he wise for the government to look towards building that road with the proceeds of sales of lands in that northern country. I would not say that the general revenue of the country should not he finally taxed for this purpose. The country might have to advance some money in the initial stages of the enterprise, but I think it should be so financed that, eventually, the land would pay for the road. I think this is a proposition for the near future. With
regard to the Georgian bay canal, I do not look forward to the building of it iu the near future or until the Transcontinental Railway is completed, and until we see what it is going to do for us with its improved grades, its straight lines, its capacity for carrying heavy loads ami its cheap rates. Until this is known, I thiuk we should not rush on with large expenditures for other transportation lines. 1 think that, possibly, the Intercolonial should be extended to the centres of Ontario, and, perhaps, to the Georgian hay. I believe also that branch lines in the eastern provinces should he considered by the government with a view to strengthening the system. These things, I think, are in the interests of Canada and the government should look in this direction.
I have read the statement by a learned English professor that, within a generation, Canada would be the centre of the empire. I confess that I cannot take so sanguine a view as that. What may come to pass in three generations or more we cannot say. But, of one thing I have no doubt, and that is that a great future is before Canada. I believe Canada has the most valuable part of the North American continent. I believe that we shall have on this northern part of the continent, a population strong and progressive-this must be the result of our climatic conditions. I see no reason why any Canadian should be pessimistic as to the future of his country or why Canadians, when a slight stringency occurs-a stringency that is far greater in other countries-should howl poverty and disaster for Canada. Our credit has stood the strain well. We find that there is a great inpouring of capital from Great Britain into Canada to-day, and here I would like to read to the House a statement of the bond issue of Canada for 1907.
