We welcome this capital, we get it cheap, use is nere and make a good deal more than the interest we have to pay upon it. The future of Canada depends largely upon getting population of the right class. 1 would say to the government:	Do not
relax the efforts to secure immigration, but bring in the people and settle them in the west. The prosperity of the west will build up the prosperity of the east. We have only to look at the result to-day of a partial failure in the west to see how one part of the country depends upon the other. Western Canada, for years to come, with ordinary success and fairly good crops, will tax the manufacturing industries of the east to their utmost capacity. How ? By the increase of its population. Not only do these people, going on the land, increase their own products, but the supplying of their needs in many lines of manufacture means prosperity for the whole country. I thank the House for the consideration shown me, in this almost my maiden speech.

There is one thing the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. McKenzie) said that I can agree with, and that is that the outlook of Canada may well be optimistic. There is no substantial ground for pessimism if, as he says, the flow of immigration continues, and we get the right sort. Every one will agree with that. But the question naturally suggests itself: We have the flow of immigration, is it of the right sort? Who is responsible if it is not the right sort ? Why, it is the government. Every one admits that a large percentage of what we are getting is not of the right sort, and yet the government are spending the money of Canada to bring in the wrong sort and fill up the country with what is entirely unsuitable. The hon. gentleman dealt with several subjects, but I have not time to do more than touch upon them. He told us one thing we did not know before with regard to the North Atlantic Trading Company. He told us that Mr. Sifton asked them to form such a company. That is new information. So I presume after this, if the hon. member from South Bruce is reliable, we may fairly Mr. McKenzie.
hold the member for Brandon responsible for the formation of that company, and whatever odium may attach to that company he is largely entitled to, because he, it seems, was one of the originators of the company, and his man Preston carried it out. The hon. member for South Bruce justifies the action of that company, lie justifies the expenditure, he justifies the secrecy surrounding the expenditure, and surrounding the so-called company, and he justifies the denial of the right to the representatives of the people in parliament to ascertain who got the $300,000 or $400,000 of Canada's money for immigrants that was paid out to this company, a large percentage of whom were entirely unsuitable for Canada. The hon. member for South Bruce holds that the' secrecy was justifiable, that it was ample for parliament to be told : If you send one or two men into a room with me I will show you the names of the individuals who form that North Atlantic Trading Company, provided you never mention them outside. I would like to ask him if he thinks his constituents would be satisfied with that. I would like to ask him if the farmers of South Bruce would be satisfied if he told them : I went into a room, I saw three or four German names and one or two English names, I do not know whether they were paupers or millionaires, whether they were in the immigration business or not, how much of Canada's money they got, whether Canada got any return for it or not; we were not allowed to go on with the inquiry because we were told that those names were to be kept absolutely secret. I ask the hon. member if he thinks his constituents would be satisfied with an explanation such as that. We were assured in this House that the expenditure of this money was all right, that it was expended by a very wealthy corporation of responsible and respectable men, a body corporate and politic, and the letters of incorporation were shown in this House as representing that respectable corporation that was incorporated in Amsterdam, with the seal on it, showing it to be a wealthy corporation, to be an honest corporation. These letters of incorporation were held up before the eyes of the people's representatives as evidence that the money had been spent by these respectable men, and we had to accept the assurance. But afterwards, when we were endeavouring to ascertain who composed that corporation, we found there was no such company iu existence, that an absolute deception had been practised upon the people's representatives-I say, to the eternal shame of the man who stood up and defended it. And the hon. member for South Bruce was satisfied with all that, and would, have been satisfied to this day, and would have gone out no doubt and told the electors of South

Bruce that this money was spent with a *wealthy incorporated company of respectable men, had the opposition in parliament not gone on and made inquiry and ascertained that no such company existed, that no such corporation had ever been formed, or were in existence at that time. The whole thing was an absolute forgery and deception. How discreditable, how disgraceful it was, and I ask the hon. member for South Bruce : Are his constituents satisfied with that ? Will they justify the government and their supporters in endeavouring to burke an inquiry with regard to that large expenditure of money on the North Atlantic Trading Company ?
Why did the government cancel the contract ?

That question has been asked. If we were getting such satisfactory results, why did the government cancel the contract ? Can the hon. member for South Bruce answer that ? Does he forget that Lord Strathcona said that we would get as many good immigrants if we never spent a dollar on that North Atlantic Trading Company ? Is he aware of the fact that since the contract was cancelled we are getting immigrants equally as good, in as large numbers, increasing numbers every year? Yet that contract-was cancelled, all expenditures were stopped, as regards that North Atlantic Trading Company, it is not operating any longer. So far as we know, Canada has not suffered in any respect by the cancellation of that contract and we are saving hundreds of thousands of dollars that we were paying out before.
The hon. gentleman has quoted Lord Strathcona. Did not Lord Strathcona justify keeping the names secret ?
I don't remember that he did, but I think he sjaid he saw no reason why the names should not be given.
I do not think so. s

But he did not agree that . we should ever enter into such a contract as that. He says in- his letter that it was against his views, but because he believed it was the policy of the party in Ottawa, and because the deputy minister came from Ottawa and associated himself with Mr. Preston and went into the organization of that company, he did not feel like going against their views, knowing also that it was the view of the Minister of the Interior, whose representatives were over there. But his judgment was that it was wrong and improper, and we would get no substantial return for it.
Did you not say we wrere paying nothing now ?
I said to the North Atlantic Trading Company.
No, you said we had been spending this money.
The Minister of Cus-ttoms is too respectable a man to try to make me say something I did not say. I said we were not spending a dollar with that North Atlantic Trading Company for that purpose.
You said we were saving the money, I think.
The money that we paid to the North Atlantic Trading Company.
But you are paying it to some one else.

We are paying it to ppople that we know, we are paying nothing to that company. Now with regard to the class of immigrants. The hon. member said : If we were getting the right class. Are we getting the right class ? Have we got the right class, and how are they placed ? Then we are paying $5 a head to bring men here who are presumably farmers.
How are you saving it then ?
That is poor saving.

It is poor saving. How has the other $600 been taken out of the country? Unfortunately, improperly, stolen! Who has prosecuted the man who did it? What has been done by the Minister of the Interior or the Minister of Agriculture ? Nothing has been done. This was going on all year until finally it was brought to the attention of the House. These men who were brought out to this country and were declared by the Department of Agriculture to be farmers and agricultural labourers were planted out among the farmers when they had never spent a day on the farm but had come from the cities and towns of England and other European countries. As farmers and agricultural labourers $5 a head was paid for them, $2 a head was paid to the agent to locate them and in many cases no immigrant was ever located. Letters from farmers were read by my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Clements) in the House today showing that this agent never earned the money which was paid to him. in one case $10, in another $12, in another $8, in many cases $5, $4 or $2 and in many of these cases no immigrant had been placed at all. And no -prosecution ! This is the country's money, is it not ? Who is responsible for the stealing of this money out of the public treasury ? The government.

Who was this agent ? The government's agent. The government, although they have ' a guilty knowledge, although they are responsible, in so far as we know, have not raised hand or foot to punish the individual who did this. Is that what the country expects from a moral government, from an honest government, a good meaning government, a government of business men ? I say it is a disgrace to any civilized country in the world. What does their own agent say in regard to many of these people coming out to Canada V What does Mr. Bruce. Walker say ? In a pamphlet which he has issued he tells us that the East End Emigration Fund has sent out 0,096 immigrants and the Central Emigration body 2,842. What do the members of the government say about that ? We have beeu told that they are bringing out nothing but the very best, that the government are exercising supervision over those that come ; that they are examined there and they are examined when they land here, both at the point of embarkation and the point of debarkation, that those who are unsuitable for Canada are sent back. But, what does Mr. Walker say ?
The Central Emigration Board, an executive body, not at all of a philanthropic or charitable character, was brought into existence for the purpose of providing a machine for booking and emigrating the products of the provincial distress committees. The latter have not taken kindly to the organization, inasmuch as provincial distress committees object to overlooking the claims of local booking agents, probably ratepayers in their community

To whom we pay $5 as well.
-in order to deal with the Central Emigration Board in London, from whom they receive no return, and no special consideration. Consequently, therefore," notwithstanding the inauguration of this body, with considerable press display, and not a little prestige from important and influential persons on the directorate, it has not done a great deal of business. During the year it sent to Canada 228 persons.
Then he says :
In inclosing you in tabulated form the totals of persons emigrated by such philanthropic societies as I have dealt with in this report, I beg to offer, in the most respectful way, the suggestion for submission to the minister, that if this emigration is not to be discouraged in toto, some means must be devised at once for its proper supervision and control.
Thereby admitting that there is no proper supervision and control over the immigrants that come here.
Mr- PATTERSON. You are in favour of that, are you uot ?
In favour of what ?
What he suggests ?

The government have been telling the country for five years that they are doing all they can and their immigration agents says they are not. That is what I want to bring to the attention of the government and of the country. What they have been declaring they were doing they are not doing at all, and it must be done if the country is not to suffer.
In my opinion, it will be an unfortunate condition of affairs if such organizations are permitted, unrestricted and unrestrained, to pour upon the shores of Canada large numbers of persons, few of whom are morally and physically quite fltted.
That is the class that are coming in.
Mr, PATERSON. No, we will not allow them to come.

Will not allow them to come? They are coming in thousands, they are filling our charitable institutions in Toronto and Montreal and, what is worse, they are filling our hospitals.
It might be well to institute a regulation that the same permission should be obtained for the emigration of such persons as is obtained for the emigration of persons from I workhouses, and it might also be permissible j to insist that such organizations in England must have a complement 'organization in Canada.
To distribute them.
Here is what one of the judges of the country said in regard to this matter in addressing the grand jury of the county of Carleton :
_ In addressing the grand jury at the opening of the high court assizes yesterday Judge MacMahon referred to the injurious results of immigrants coming into Canada who were not mentally sound. He read statements of Dr. C. K. Clarke, superintendent of the Toronto asylum, to the effect that of the 362 admissions to that institution last year 136 were foreign born. The majority were recent arrivals. Of these most were deported but there were about 40 that the province would never get rid of, - and each patient that is retained would cost the province $6,000.
That is only speaking of one of the cities of Canada.
The Provincial Secretary's Department has deported thirty since January last. Of these weak-minded foreigners, sixty-live per cent were afflicted with dimentia prjecox, the same form of insanity accredited to Harry
K.	Thaw.
And this is a class for which we are paying $5 a head when we should be filling up the country with desirable citizens. These were the most undesirable classes of lunatics and were likely to live a great many years. In other words they were the failures sent from the old country by immigration companies to try and make good in Canada if possible. The judge explained that this disease was usually contracted In early life,

and in 60 per cent of the cases becomes evident before the age of twenty-five years.
And that is the class we are bringing in in such large numbers. Mr. Bruce Walker also speaks of this class and condemns the policy that had been carried out for the last five years during which time the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Agriculture have been telling Canada that the government were exercising the greatest care in the selection of immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend said that we paid $5 a head for these.
I said for some of these.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The mere fact that these people came in does not prove that we paid $5 a head.

I reached that conclusion because they are taken right to the farms in the country and come out as farm labourers. I know that they are brought out as farm labourers and were booked as such, because they said they were advised to put themselves down as farm labourers, although they had never worked a day on the farm. I have had four or five in my own employ and I do not think that they had worked on a farm before.
Were they crazy?
Some of them were, not the ones I had, however, and we raised money and sent them to Toronto. They were Imbeciles.
Did the Ontario government bring them out; did not they place the men on the farms?

I made application at Toronto and I think the application was forwarded here and they were sent on to me as soon ns they landed by the immigration agent for the Dominion. Three of them were sent on. As far as I know, they were sent from the immigrants brought in by the Dominion. They told me that they were instructed to book themselves as going on farms, although they had never worked on farms.
You had better mention that to Mr. Whitney.
I mention it to the people responsible, to the people who did it, who spent the people's money ; I mention it to the guilty parties.
Was their information reliable, if they were crazy?
I did not say that the men I had were crazy ; I said the men who were brought into our locality and put among the farmers were in some cases crazy and some were sent to Toronto.
Were they the ones you were talking to.

No. I think the hon. member for Ottawa will have to put an insurance policy on this man or he will explode again. At the meeting of the Associated Charities in Toronto it was said that the medical inspection was ' farcical.' This was stated by Dr. Hodgetts, I believe. Mr. Samuel Arnold, secretary of the Associated Charities, at the same meeting gave a statement of the position of the allied societies. This was in September last, really before the season of the year when distress is felt in the cities. The statement was as follows:
St. Andrew's Society, he said, had not one family to provide for. The Society of St. Vincent de Paul suggested that men with families should have enough funds to support them for six months. St. George's Society assisted persons 681 times-
M'hat city is that?

Toronto, last September.
-sent nine to the hospital, and had seven funerals in the past year. On the register of the British Welcome League there were 5,293 names. . Of these, 603 were without money, 347 with less than $2, 310 with over $2 but less than $5, 185 married couples with 352 children, wthout cash, 318 couples with 865 children with less than $5 a family.
They had been landed down in Canada and at once became practically paupers on the country. These were the desirable immigrants that the government * were bringing out to the country.
During the past year 30D persons applied for work at the office of the Associated Charities, and of these over 200 were recent arrivals. At the city hall 216 persons asked for relief and 44 for hospital treatment. All had lived less than three months in the country.
And that is the class we are paying so much money to bring into Canada.
Does it say the Ontario government brought them out?
What is the million dollars being spent for by this government? To bring them out and to pay bonuses.
I am asking you

-to pay bonuses to the booking companies and many of these were brought out as desirable settlers.
Out of 200 families aided by the House of Industry, 150 were immigrants.
Rev. Canon Welsh appealed for quality, not quantity, in immigration, and said immigrants should have definite employment guaranteed them before they left home.

Hudson showed that on paper the rules of the Dominion government for the medical inspection of immigrants were excellent, but in practice they were execrable.
The discussion was continued by Dr. Pepler, Mr. W. P. Sexton, Mr. J. C. Bayliss, Mr. C. W. Mogridge, Mr. H. M. Mowat, K.C., and Mr. G. E. Harman.
Dr. Hodgetts said that the medical examination of the immigrants was farcical, as a

physician was not allowed time sufficient to properly examine all who passed through his hands. Cases of heart and lung diseases and even of imbecility frequently escaped their notice.
That is the class of men who are being brought to the country and we are expected to applaud the government because they are bringing them to Canada. What is the result to-day ? It is that there are over
2,000	people in Toronto out of employment. I saw in a paper no longer ago than yesterday that two or three of these men had been offered $25 a month and their board to work on farms near Toronto, and refused because they could not get $26 a month. These men are lying about the towns and cities of Canada and are absolutely useless to go on farms. They have no sense of honour and no regard for a bargain, whether it is written or oral. Large numbers of them come from London, and they tell us they never worked on a farm; yet they are sent out as farmers. I employed one on a farm, and I saw him walk around a field three times to learn how to put in a plough, and he could not manage it properly if he got a million dollars. I was to pay him $20 a month, with board and washing.
The Ontario government brought him out. You should mention Hie matter to Whitney.

He told me he was booked at the Dominion government agency in London. I have had three more of them since. I had one who left only last week, who had been paid $20 a month, with board and washing, ail winter, although I do not think he was worth half that. He went away on Saturday night, and never came back, and he is now looking for work. Another remained three days ; another remained nine days. This is the kind of immigration the hon. member eulogized. Some years ago in the Committee on Agriculture the hon. member moved a resolution recommending the government to try to get the embargo taken off cattle, and he stood up with the greatest simplicity and innocence and assurances to tell the Committee that the government of England was going to change shortly, he believed, and a reform government was going to come in and would take the embargo off cattle. That reform government came in. Has it taken off the embargo yet ? How many times has the Minister of Agriculture applied to it, but he has not succeeded. Have we heard anything about it since? Not a word lately. If the hon gentleman is a prophet. I am afraid he is one of the false prophets. He talked a great deal about the cold storage provided by the Minister of Agriculture and told us what beneficial results we had from it. He said that practically all our products, including cheese and butter and eggs, were sent in cold storage and were therefore sold at a higher price in the British market Mr. SPROULE.
than before. Am I correct in that my understanding of his contention ?
I spoke more particularly of early apples and small fruits during the months of August and September.
I thought he mentioned cheese, butter and egggs.
In reply to Mr. E. D. Smith. Of course, I accept the statement of the hon. gentleman as the truth.

The hon. gentleman accepts my statement as correct. Then what did the Minister of Agriculture say in this House in answer to a question by Mr. Armstrong ? This is the question :
What was the total number of boxes of cheese, butter, eggs, bacon, apples, in boxes and barrels respectively, shipped in cold storage, the number in cooled air chambers, and the number shipped in ordinary storage in twelve months previous to March 1, 1908?
What was the answer to that ? Here is what the Minister of Agriculture said :
Of the cheese sent over in cold storage, there was not a single box in the twelve months; in cooled air chambers, 290,076 boxes; but in ordinary storage, 1,721,000 boxes.
I would like to ask the hon. member if lie expects cheese to be shipped in cold storage. You can ship but ter in cold storage, but you destroy cheese if you ship it too cold.

Did not the hon. member state the benefit that the farmers .were receiving from it, and did he not admit that what I stated practically represented his sentiment ? How much butter went over in cold storage ? 66,S96 boxes. I take meats; how many boxes went in cold storage ? 2,858. How many in cooled air chambers ?
29,000.	How many in ordinary storage ? 25,900. Take lard-how much went in cold storage ? Not a single pound. How much in ordinary storage ? 1,000 packages. Then I take apples, which the hon. member says cold storage is for ; how many went over in cold storage ? 6,131 barrels. How many in cooled air chambers, 1,720 barrels. How many in ordinary storage ? 634,000 barrels. There is what the farmers got from this splendid system of cold storage.

Surely the hon. gentleman does not expect the whole trade of Canada to go in cold storage. Surely he must know as well as I that during the latter part of the summer, when our winter apples are going forward^ there is no necessity for cold storage. That is required for the earlier apples and perishable fruit.

Then why did the hon. gentleman misrepresent the facts by saying that practically it all went by cold storage? He said that nearly all the apples went in

cold storage, but I have shown him that by far the greater proportion went without cold storage. When the farmers of South Bruce read what he said and then compare his statement with the facts, what credit will he receive from them? Of the tender fruit, how much went in cold storage? None at all. How many eggs went in cool air chambers? 931 boxes. How many in the ordinary way, without cold storage at all ?	24.249 boxes. And the
farmers are expected to bow down and be grateful to the Minister of Agriculture. I see that the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) Is here. What did he say on that question? He also eulogized the Minister of Agriculture for the wonderful things he had accomplished by his cold storage, and he went on to say that practically all that the farmers sent now was sent in cold storage, and their products were consequently laid down in splendid condition in the markets of the world. The hon. member for Eambton (Mr. Armstrong) put to him this question: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that all these articles he has mentioned were exported in cold storage ? And the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) replied: That is my understanding and my opinion. But I have given the facts to show how utterly absurd his opinion was. Then the hon. member for South Grey went on to give a list of figures, showing the quantity of eggs and butter and cheese and bacon and hams exported, and he left the inference to be drawn that all these went in cold storage. The hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) again asked him if these were all exported in cold storage, and the hon. gentleman replied:	That is my understanding. But we find that exactly the contrary is the case. What has the hon. member for South Grey to say, in the face of the 'figures given by the Minister of Agriculture to-day? If the farmers of South Grey only heard the one side, they might believe the hon. gentleman, but if the facts are put before them what will they think of him? They will conclude that either he is absolutely ignorant or dishonest-that he either does not know the facts or is dishonest enough to give figures which the facts do not bear out for the purpose of making some political advantage for himself and party and his wonderful Minister of Agriculture.
Cold storage is a good thing, is it not? Whether they ship by cold storage or not, is it not a good thing? Or are you opposed to it?

The hon. minister from Brant (Mr. Paterson) is very fond of putting -I was going to say silly-'but I will say irrelevant questions. I do not like to be offensive but I cannot see the sense of his putting the questions he does. We have had held up to us the action of the government in furnishing seed as a great boon to 210
the farmers of the west. Well, a great many of the farmers do not approve of the system the government have adopted. It would have been far better if the government had made some arrangement by which the farmers, whose crops were a failure, could have been furnished with the money with which to buy seed from their neighbours, whose crops were not frost bitten and who consequently had seed for sale. Take one section where the grain was destroyed by the frost and adjoining that you will find another where the grain was first-class and where those farmers, whose crops had failed, could get all the seed they required if they had the money to pay for it. But instead of doing this the government are providing the seed themselves and taking security for payment from the farmers, and the government are giving a bonus of 3 cents a bushel in the way of a higher price for it to those who will turn in pure seed. Who is getting that bonus? A good manv of the friends of the government are getting it and those who are not friends are not getting it. That discrimination is wrong. In any event the price of seed grain is raised 3 cents a bushel and the farmer who requires it has to pay that. His neighbour who has equally good grain cannot sell it to him because he has not the money to pay for it, and he is compelled to take the government grain and pay 3 cents a bushel more. I am not giving this as an argument of my own. I had it from a man in Saskatchewan who is farming there. He has in his granery as fine wheat as you coutd wish to see yet he cannot sell lo the farmers, who are in want of seed, because they have not the money to pay for it. Those farmers are obliged to give the government security and have to pay from 3 cents to 5 cents more per bushel for grain which is no better or cleaner than they could get from adjoining farms. I am not blaming the government so much because I think that was not what they intended. I believe they were doing their best, but when we are doing our best, it does not always work out exactly right. This man said to me that if the" government had provided some means whereby the farmers could get money enough to buy from their neighbours, they could buy equally as good grain and very much cheaper. But to-day they have either to do without the grain or give security and buy from the government at a much higher price.
Was it known that the grain you speak of was all right? Was it tested?
It was wheat which no man with an eye in his head and who was a farmer could doubt was first-class wheat.
They say the oats that were blighted looked just as well.

You could be deceived easily in oats but not in wheat.

Is the hon. gentleman aware that the people appreciate the fact that they can get outside grain and prefer to pay 3 cents more per bushel for it.
The government can get as good grain in the country.
They do not want to get it from their neighbours but want to change the seed.

That is largely moon-sliinei Besides most of the wheat is not imported at all but bought in the country there. I wish now to refer to the discussion which took place this afternoon. My hon. friend from West Kent (Mr. Clements) was dealing with a very important subject, and during most of the time he spoke there -was but one minister present. I do not know whether the ministers have entirely abandoned their functions as such, but the House sat with only one minister present and he a subordinate one, although at the moment the government were being charged with dereliction of duty and improper conduct. The benches were empty nearly the whole afternoon and but one minister present.
Mr. iMcKENZIE. Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? While he was speaking it struck me very forcibly-would it not be well to refer to the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) for his absence ? This country is paying that hon. gentleman a good salary and he has been in his place very little within the last month.

It is not against the leader of the opposition that charges are made, but against the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Immigration, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) is not responsible for these.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clements) give notice to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) of any such charge to be made?
Some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not very defiuite.
I heard him in his place give notice to the House that it was his intention

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the kind of notice that is due to a minister. He should get notice of the time when the matter is to be brought up.
That is the kind of notice that any member should give and It is all the government should ask or expect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. iSproule).
I am speaking from a knowledge of some years which is worth as much to me as the experience of the min-

ister (Mr. Fielding) is to him. Here are charges made against the Department of Immigration, not merely of mismanagement but of absolute fraud in the expenditure of public money. Yet we do not learn of any effort made to compel restitution, or to punish the parties. The hon. member (Mr. Clements) read case after case, seven hundred in all, of people for whom the agent had received a commission of $2 a head. And when letters were addressed to the individuals who were supposed to have taken these employees, half of them declared that they had never had these men. Yet this agent got $1,200 for locating these people, half of whom were never located at all;- pure dishonesty. And, that charge being-brought to the attention of the government, they have not a word of reply, but sit as dumb as oysters. They do not try to punish the individual, or get back the money, or offer any excuse. But is it any wonder that this individual should act in this way? I do not think so. He knowTs what is going on in the departments of the government. Everybody who deals with the government expects to get a rake-off or to steal some of the public money. And the man who gets only a small portion feels that he is hardly doing himself justice because somebodv else is more astute than he and gets a larger amount. Now, not only wms $2 a head paid for locating these people in this country, but $5 a head was paid for bringing them here, and this was done on the plea that they were farm labourers. Yet what do these lettters show that were read by the hon. member (Mr. Clements)? One man had never worked as a farmer, but was a plasterer by trade; another had been a mechanic; another stayed a few days and then went and got work in Detroit. And these were the people that were sent out as farm hands, labourers, $5 per head being paid to bring them here and $2 a head to locate them, though many were not located at all. And yet the government has not a word to say. Was this not a fraud? It would appear that somebody buncoed the government, but no attempt seems to be made to punish the parties. What percentage of these people belong to the agricultural class? Not half of them. In fact, half of them were not located at all. so that probably not more than one-quarter of these people were agriculturists. This shows the slipshod methods employed by the department, which are also illustrated in the examining of immigrants at the port of debarkation.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is said to be a practical farmer, a man *whose ambition it is to do something for the farmers of this country. He often tells what a wonderful thing he did in getting the United States regulations changed so as to enable us to get our cattle sent into that country, and this is how it works out at the

present time. If the hon. gentleman disbelieve me, my hon. friend from Russell (.Mr. N. F. Wilson), whom I saw at the gathering of livestock men the other day, will verify what I say. Here for instance is the regulation with regard to horses-it provides how these horses may be brought into Canada :
A proper pedigree referring to the English or American stud-book to be given by the breeder in his certificate, but in the case of such blood horses whose pedigree is not entered in the stud-book an authenticated certificate of purity of blood and identification will be sufficient, provided the animal is found on inspection to have the properties and qualifications essential to improvement of breed.
Then, as to short-horn cattle :
The breeders' certificate shall embody a correct pedigree, referring to a recognized shorthorn herd book.
These regulations were made in November, 1887, before the present government came into power. And yet, they have been telling the farmers of the wonderful things the Minister of Agriculture accomplished by going to Washington and arranging with the Secretary of Agriculture for an exchange of pure-bred cattle between Canada and the Vnited States. I find in the ' Farmers' Advocate ' of Manitoba announcement of a sale of pure-bred cattle at Wetaskiwin, on March 31. And where are the cattle from? They are from the United States. They are consigned to a Canadian who sells them in his own name. These are advertised as pure-bred cattle, and the farmer who buys them thinks he is getting cattle that can be registered here in the herd-book of Canada. He goes on and buys them and what does he find? He buys them as purebred cattle, and he finds that they won't register here at all. Thejr have four registration herd books over there, they belong to joint stock companies who make money out of the business. Therefore they are lax in it, and we would not admit their registration at all. But the cattle they are bringing in and pretending to be pure-bred cattle as we know and understand the term, are cattle that cannot be registered in Canada. Will the Americans allow us to do that with our cattle? We are sending cattle over there and what do they compel us to do? They compel us to register our cattle before they get in, and it costs $100 a head to register. But we allow them to bring theirs in here free, and they sell their cattle in Canada as pure-bred, and we find that they are only grades when wet get them. So the Canadian farmer is deceived and imposed upon, a fraud is perpetrated upon him, and our beautiful Minister of Agriculture is letting it go on.
Does he know about it ?

Yes, he was at the meeting, and they brought it to his attention, and they asked for a remedy. I asked the question the other day : Are the government taking any steps to regulate this, and under what regulations are the cattle coming in now ? The Minister of Agriculture did not answer, but the Minister of Customs answered, and said they were coming in under the same regulations as in 1887. Yet the Minister of Agriculture told the farmers of this country in the meantime, I fancy a hundred times: What a blessing it is that you have me as Minister of Agriculture, because he went down to Washington and had one consultation with the Minister of Agriculture there, and arranged everything on a fair basis so that there was a free interchange between the two countries in thoroughbred stock, and grade stock as well, to the advantage of farmers in Canada. Now they bring in horses, what are they wrorth when they bring them in ? I am told they are no good, the horses cannot register here. I say that also is a fraud perpetrated upon the farmers of Canada, and it becomes a tax placed on our good cattle. Our farmers are paying three prices for them. One case is cited of a man who paid $2,100 for a horse that the party who referred to it declared on his judgment was not worth $.700. Yet these horses come in under the regulations, the Minister of Agriculture knows it, and he is making no effort to change it, and the farmers are suffering in consequence. Yet we are told by the hon. member for South Bruce and others that we ought to be profoundly thankful because we have a practical farmer at the head of the department.
Does the hon. member mean to state that all thoroughbred cattle going over to the States to be sold come under this hundred dollar regulation ?
The man that was trying to ship them was told that he could not take them in unless he paid $100, he had either to give it then, or to pay it beforehand.

The cattle that pay this $100 registration fee in order to be sold in the States are cattle of recent importation. I know the cattle we have bred and sold in the States have been registered before this clause was adopted requiring a hundred dollars to be paid, and we don't pay anything extra in order to sell in the States.
When was that clause enacted ?

Two years ago. Up to the time of our national registration we registered all our cattle in the American Shorthorn herd book.
