If they are registered there, of course you could take them there. But now they have to be taken in by an American, and they have to be registered as well-so I am informed, and if am not correct I want to be set right. That is the regulation, and I complain because the Minister of Agriculture allows American cattle to come in under such a regulation on their side, while we are deprived of the benefit of their market, and the Minister of Agriculture sits by and allows Canadian farmers to suffer.
Now as we are practically discussing the budget, I wish to sa'J' a few words about the speech of the hon. member for Brandon. I was amused to see how highly the reform press eulogized that speech. You would think it was one of the most wonderful deliverances ever heard in the House of Commons. It was original, it was new, it was practical, it was valuable, and if it was carried out, what wonderful benefits would result to Canada. Well, if all this is true, is it not a condemnation of the government who waited all these years for the hon. member for Brandon to tell them what they should do ? In proportion as Ills deliverances were wise and his recommendations valuable, in the same proportion did he condemn his late colleagues because they have not been doing what he says they should do. His whole speech is a rebuke to the government. He says that several reforms are urgently demanded, and not one of them was mentioned in the speech from the Throne or in the budget speech. Not a word in the speech from tile Throne about building the Hudson Bay railway, not a word about his other propositions, excejit something about the all-red line in the budget speech. Now is there any justification for the fulsome eulogies of that speech by the Reform press ? Were these suggestions new ? Not one of them was new, they had been discussed in this House over and over again. What are they ? Reforming the Department of Trade and Commerce by the appointment of commercial agents to increase our trade. What were we told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce? They were going to establish commercial agencies all over the world, who would collect statistical data that would be of great value, they were going to increase immensely our foreign trade ; and that the Department of Trade and Commerce was going to do wonderful things that had never been done before. But the member for Brandon says it wants to be reorganized ; it is out of date. We have paid sufficient money to enable the government to get it up to date. We have 32 or 33 agents appointed in England, South Africa, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and other countries and yet the hon. member from Brandon tells us they are no use. We want it reorgan-Mr. N. F. WILSON.
ized and that is what the country needs to-day. If it has not got it who is to be condemned ? The government told us when they organized the department and agreed to pay $7,000 a year to the head of it that they were going to have wonderful results from it, but the hon. member for Bra-ndon tells us: We never had any wonderful results. Is that not a condemnation of the government ? Certainly it is, and they must be responsible for it. The next question referred to by the hon. gentleman was that of civil service reform. We have had civil service reform discussed over and over again since I came into this House thirty years ago. Every year some one is going to reform the civil service. Before the Conservative government went out they appointed a commission and they were prepared to reform the service and woud have done so if they had not gone out of power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. They did not go out of power for nearly four years after that. The commission was appointed in 1891 and made its report in 1892. They made no reform at all.	.
On account of going out of power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They had all the time they needed but they did not do it.*

I am not going to debate that now. The present government have been in office for twelve years. They have had two civil service commissions and they have not reformed the civil service. Yet, the hon. member for Brandon says that it should be reformed. Is that not a condemnation of his own friends ? On the contrary, they have deformed it. They have been in office for twelve years and there is no result as yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have had the report of the commission for three weeks and the late government had the report of their commission for four years and did nothing.
But you had a commission before this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Never.
Yes, they reported long ago and you introduced two measures in consequence of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken ; there was no commission.
What was it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no commission. I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to.
There was the inquiry upon which you based your Superannuation and Pension Fund Bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend lias made a statement and lie is questioning about some other things. He has said that we have had two commissions. I say that he is mistaken. There has been no commission but the one that was recently appointed and which has reported.
I will give my hon. friend the facts later.
When Sir .Win. Muloek introduced the Superannuation Bill there was no commission.
By the government, I suppose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every Bill is the subject of inquiry.

The next question that came up was the fast Atlantic service. When the present government came into power there was a provisional abstract made for a fast Atlantic service which called for an annual payment of $7501000, but the present government declared that they could provide a service for $500,000 a year, and that they would not pay $750,000. Man after man got up and said that we did not want a fast Atlantic service, that we required something to carry freight and it did not matter whether it was carried rapidly so long as it was carried cheaply. They took two grounds, first, that we did not need it, and, second, that we were paying too much for it. Now. we are told by this wonderful Daniel-come-to-judgment that it is the most pressing need of the times and that it would be cheap for Canada to give $1,226,000 for it, the only difference being that it will extend across the Pacific as well as the Atlantic. This wonderful thing is something new, something great. They are all talking about it now. The press have eulogized the deliverance of the hon. member for Brandon for advocating something that was practically ready to be realized some twelve years ago but which the government, with its want of foresight and good judgment, prevented from being accomplished. The government refused to ratify the contract which was made by their predecessors, they declared the service was not needed and now we are told that it is one of the most pressing neeus of the country. The next was the building of the Hudson Bay Railway. I listened to members from the Northwest the other day saying how much they wanted it. I believe they do want it. When I was in Winnipeg five years ago I was asked by the ' Free Press ' if I would give them an interview on what the country needed and I said that one of the most urgent needs of the time was the Hudson Bay Railway. I was taken to task very severely by a good many people on
both sides of politics for saying so. That was my opinion then and it is my opinion still. Now the hon. member for Brandon comes forward as an advocate of this project forgetting that the only effort that was ever made to build that road was by the late government. If they had remained in power the whole of the road would undoubtedly have been built long ago but because they went out the present government have allowed the men who held the subsidy and charter to dilly-dally with it. They have renewed the subsidy and kept it alive but the railway is not built and it never will be built so long as the laxity of the present government continues.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the Hudson Bay Railway is being built and that it is already built for a considerable distance ?

I am aware that a portion of road which is used for other purposes is being built as part of a line going to the Pacific coast. Can the hon. gentleman tell me how much is built and how much they got to build it ? I do not think he knows anything about it. He has heard some one tell him. What a wonderful inspiration it was that came from the superlative cranium of the hon. member for Brandon when he said that the road might bo built by setting aside a portion of the land ! Practically the late government were carrying out the same principle in giving alternate sections of land for the purpose of building it. What is the difference ? The member for Brandon says hold the land for, say ten years, until it becomes valuable. If you hold the land for ten years it may become valuable but there is the interest accruing on the money in the meantime. The only practical effort that was made to build the road was made by the Conservative party. These are the wonderful deliverances of the hon. member for Brandon. The last was that the government should buy back the lands from the railways and throw them open for settlement. We have discussed that in the House a dozen times and a dozen years ago. Every one of these old subjects has been revived and revamped, and the utterances of the hon. gentleman with regard to them are considered to be a wonderful deliverance as If be were an oracle from Heaven. Every Liberal paper praises the hon. gentleman and in proportion as it .praises him it condemns its own friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the Tory papers praised him.

Yes, and I said they were slobbering over nothing. I have heard it discussed so often. There was not a suggestion made in the speech that was not debated over and over again in this House, and the fact that they are not ful-
6G15

filled to-day is in several instances due entirely to the present government who had It in their power to carry them out. The late government were prepared to carry out the suggestions had they remained in power, and would have carried them out long before this. If the people do not to-day enjoy these advantages it is because of the men-I was going to say the incompetents -who have occupied the treasury benches for the past eleven years. I would not have spoken upon this question had it not been that the government have not dared to utter one word in defence or justification of this, or to say what they are going to do with regard to the stealing of the money of the country, the dishonest conduct of their own employees.

This debate, Mr. Speaker, has taken a very wide range. Hon. gentlemen opposite have gone back into ancient history and have made many gloomy predictions as to the future ; but not one of them, to my mind, has made any fair attempt to meet the splendid statement made in ,the budget speech of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).
Is this the budget debate ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You might ask the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Clements) who said that he was cut out on the budget debate and was now cutting in.

The story which the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) had to tell was heard with delight by every patriotic Canadian. It was a story of increasing trade, increasing prosperity, increasing deposits in the savings banks, improved transportation facilities, a surplus on the Intercolonial Railway, a surplus in the post office and a surplus in the general revenue of the country, the largest in the history of Canada. With all these evidences of prosperity before them my hon. friends have made more blue-ruin speeches than it has ever before been my misfortune to listen to. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) went pretty far; he saw all kinds of bogies across his path, but the past master as a blue-ruin prophet was the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt). There was nothing too doleful for that hon. gentleman. The lamentations of Jeremiah were cheerful reading compared to that hon. gentleman's remarks in this debate. If there is one thing more than another characteristic of the Canadian people it is that they are hopeful, that they look forward with great courage and hope to the future, and that they have no use for the pessimist, for the man who sees nothing but blue ruin ahead of the country. My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) to-night made a very eloquent Mr. SPROULE.
reference to the ship of slate. Let me tell these hon. gentlemen that the people of Canada will never commit the care of the ship of state to a lot of Jonahs, a number of whom mutinied the last time they had charge of her, who are always afraid to get outside the harbour and always see breakers ahead, whereas in fact the sky is clear, and the wind fair and the ship is sailing along on her triumphant course, steered by a pilot who has weathered many a storm, who still has a steady hand on the tiller and in whom the people of Canada, the owners of the ship, have implicit confidence. I sympathize with hon. gentlemen opposite in the fact that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has left them nothing to talk about, that he has exhausted the whole subject. He went over every thing that a man could possibly discuss in connection with the budget debate, leaving nothing at all for the men who sit to his right and left.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is referring to a previous debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who preceded him (Mr. Sproule) did nothing but refer to a previous debate and why should not my hon. friend enjoy the same privilege ?

It was open to my hon. friend to take the point. I will answer the question of the Minister of Finance. It is now twelve o'clock at night and I do not think the members are desirous of listening to a written essay such as is being given by the hon. member for Guysboro, who is reading his speech. For that reason I rise to the point of order in order that we may not have such a speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for West Kent (Mr. Clements) was permitted to enter upon the budget debate ; every one who has spoken to-night has done so and I submit that it is now too late to object.
I have the right to raise the point whenever I see fit.

I intend dealing with questions discussed by the last speaker (Mr. Sproule). That gentleman referred at great length to the question of immigration and endeavoured to condemn the policy of the government in regard to the paying of bonuses on immigrants. I understood from him-I do not know whether he intended to convey that idea to the House-that he was under the impression that the government were paying bonuses on all immigrants coming into Canada.
No.
Was I not speaking most of the time of farmers and farm labourers on \thom they do pay bonuses ?

He said they represented themselves as farmers and farm labourers, and found their way into this country in that way. He said that the government had paid bonuses on these people. Would he be surprised to find that the government had paid bonuses on only a small proportion of the immigrants who have come into Canada in the last eleven' years ? I find from the record that from 1897 to 31st December, 1907 we received in Canada from northern Europe 359,575 immigrants, and paid bonuses on only 27 per cent of that number.
Did that include the North Atlantic Trading Company ?

That included all the immigrants we received from Northern Europe, not including the British Islands, during that period. My hon. friend will also note that a great many people came into Canada from other parts of Europe on whom the government did not pay any bonus. Hon. gentlemen opposite appear to think the government have been paying bonuses on people coming from southern Europe, whereas they have never at any period paid bonuses on such immigrants.
Would the hon. member explain what he means by southern Europe ?
I mean the countries of southern Europe, such as Italy and Greece.
What about Rou-mania, Bulgaria and Transylvania?

I stated that the government never paid bonuses on any immigrants coming from countries of southern Europe. For every man on whom the government paid a bonus they got a settler on the western lands. They have placed more homesteaders on the lands of the west than the number of men on whom they have paid bonuses. If hon. gentlemen will examine the records of the Interior Department, they will find that while bonuses were paid on 27 per cent of the immigrants from northern Europe, 28 per cent of these immigrants settled on the lands of the west. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, they paid out a great deal of money to bring people to this country, but got almost no settlers, so that after eighteen years the western prairies were still a wilderness, while we have this splendid record,- that for every man from northern Europe on whom a bonus was paid we have settled a man on the western prairie. So
we have not lost one dollar of the bonuses we have paid. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) wishes to know the countries from which the people come on whom bonuses are paid. Under the present arrangement the government pays bonuses on three classes of immigrants- farmers, railway navvies and female domestic servants coming from the i following countries : Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Holland, Fiance, Belgium, Germany and Finland in northern Europe, and also from the British isles. My hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), in his speech the other day, informed the House that we ought to be paying bonuses on people coming from Germany. I was surprised to find the hon. gentleman, who is supposed to be an authority on German questions, making a statement like that. I do not know whether there are any Germans in his constituency but I suppose there are, and his speeches must be for them.

I might take the liberty of informing the hon. gentleman that the hon. member for East Lambton has no Germans in his riding. He talks on the basis of principle. I know it is a surprise to the hon. gentleman to find him doing so.

I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but I would like to have some explanation of the deep interest the hon. member for Lambton takes in the Germans. This is what he said in regard to immigration :
Then, Sir, on account of the present regulations of this government, within the last eleven years the immigration into Canada frein Germany has been little or nothing, and 1 am sure there is not a man in this House but who realizes the importance of a German community in any country such as Canada. Instead of us assisting immigrants to come i1 om southern parts of Europe it would be better for us to get into better relations with Germany
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise the point of order again. The hon. gentleman is referring to a previous debate. I would like to have your ruling on that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, the rule is well understood, that there cannot be any reference to a past debate. But this afternoon and this evening it seems to have been accepted by the House, commencing with the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. Clements) that the budget debate should be practically continued, and I have been assuming up to this point that that was the disposition of the House. If the point of order is pressed, I shall of course have to rule that there cannot be any reference to a past debate.
If I may be permitted, the hon. Minister of Finance and I think the Speaker rather misquoted me in saying that I referred to the budget debate. I did not treat on it to any extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was obliged to leave the House to receive an important deputation, and as I left I distinctly heard the hon. gentleman state that he had some observations to make in the budget debate, which he now wished to continue. I admit that the hon. gentleman cannot make the quotation. We have been on the budget debate the whole afternoon.
I was pointing out that the hon. member for East Lambton condemned the government for paying bonuses on immigrants from southern Europe.
The hon. gentleman is doing the same thing again. If he proposes to do that, I propose each time to raise the question of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member refers to a past debate and the point of order is pressed, I shall have to rule that he cannot do so.

I am simply discussing the question which the hon. member for East Grey discussed. If any hon. gentleman asserts that the government has been paying bonuses on immigrants coming from southern Europe, he is mistaken. There has never been such a policy. If any hon. gentleman is under the impression that the government is not now bonusing immigrants from Germany as well as from other countries of northern Europe, he ought to try and inform himself on that question, and when an hon. gentleman gets up in the House and tells us what we ought to do. when it happens to be the very thing we are now doing we are surprised.
Has this government an agent in Germany?

I understand that the policy of the government is to pay bonuses to booking agents in Germany or anywhere else in northern Europe-that since the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company has been cancelled, any booking agent in northern Europe who sends an immigrant to Canada, and succeeds in settling that immigrant on the lands of Canada, is entitled, after the immigrant has become a citizen of Canada, but not before, to the $5 for securing the immigrant, provided the immigrant is a farmer, a railway navvy or a domestic servant.
Is $5 the bonus today ?
I understand that it is.
Has it not been doubled ?
I think the hon. gentleman will find that is the bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says so.
I was informed it was that some time ago. It is a little more now.

I am afraid there is a good deal of misapprehension, not only among hon. gentlemen opposite but in the country with regard to this question of immigration. I was very much suprised the other day to see an article in the Toronto ' Globe,' on the front page of that paper, framed in a pretty way and headed with large letters ' The Goth is at our gates ' and giving the name of some Italian who had murdered some other Italian somewhere in the province of Ontario and suggesting that the government should not pay bonuses on immigrants from southern Europe. I was surprised to find that such a well informed paper should haye been led astray, but the reason is hon. gentlemen opposite from day to day make these statements in this House and the Conservative press repeat them, and the result is that they deceive the very elect, and the people run away with the idea that our immigration policy is altogether different than what it really is. I have xiointed out to the House that out of all the immigrants we have received from northern Europe, we have only paid bonuses on the 27 per cent who have settled on our lands. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Bin ini asked some questions a few days ago and got a reply, and since then the matter has not been referred to by my hon. friend, but the question he asked was such an interesting one and the answer was so interesting that I wish to place both on record :

1.	How many immigrants of every kind arrived in Canada each year since 1896?
2.	On how many immigrants has a bonus of any kind been paid in each year since 1896 ?

speakeroldname: Hon. PRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Are the immigrants from the United States included in that ?
I think so.

What calculation was made with regard to the bonuses on these immigrants? The government pay $3 a

head on what they get from the States, but I suppose they are not Included in that as bonus paid immigrants.

I am endeavouring to expose the fallacy that we have paid bonuses on all the immigrants who have come in. I do not wish the hon. gentleman to run away with the idea that when he finds a crazy man in some part of Ontario who happens to be a newcomer, we have paid a bonus on that man. Some of the crazy men he discovers in parts of Ontario are most likely men on whom we did not pay a bonus at all.
Is there a calculation showing that we have paid a bonus on the Americans or not? My understanding is that we paid $3 a head to the agent who gets them. If that is not a bonus, I do not know what is.

True we are paying a bonus of so much a head but only on certain classes and we have only paid on a very small proportion of the whole. What does the hon. gentleman want? Does he want to build a stone wall around the country and keep out these immigrants. The Department of the Interior is taking great care in the selection of immigrants. I have watched them arrive at the port of Quebec. Every man was examined by a doctor. I heard the questions asked as they went through the turnstile, and none were allowed to pass unless fit to pass examination. A large number were sent back and the greatest care was exercised by the officers of the department. What is the policy of my hon. friends opposite regarding immigrants or have they any policy at all? Do they condemn the policy of paying a small bonus of $5 on a farmer who will settle Tm our western land and help to defray the burden of taxation ? Do they remember that the debt of this country per head has been reduced by the fact that the policy of the Interior Department has been so vigorous. When they were In power the debt per head was $50, but because so many immigrants have come into the country, the debt per head to-day is only $42. Do my hon. friends remember that ? What is their policy I would like to know ? They have condemned the government, but I do not think they are justified in condemning the government for paying a small bonus of $5 for farmers who settle on the western land. Farmers are necessary out west to till the soil and so are navvies to build our railways. Then there is a great demand for female domestic servants. Our fellow citizens in British Columbia paid $400,000 into the revenue of the country to introduce Chinamen to do the domestic work of that province during the past year. That is the condition throughout Canada.
I do not think that my hon. friends, if they face this question squarely, will condemn the government for their present policy. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said we did not get the right kind of immigrants. Well, we are paying $5 a head for every respectable farmer from Ireland who comes to this country. Are they the right class of immigrants ? I have heard it said that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) claims to be of Irish descent. Does he object to immigrants coming from Ireland ? Are there no good men there ? Or what does he mean by condemning the payment of $5 a head for farmers from Ireland ?
I did not object to that. The hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) is merely setting up an argument of his own to answer it in his own way.

Is not the farmer from England all right ? The hon. gentleman dilated for a long time on the class of immigrants from London. Well, are we going to shut out a man from this country because he happened to be born in'London ? The hon. gentleman says that we ought to be condemned for letting men come here from the cities. Well, if a man is so unfortunate as to be born in a city is he to be kept outside the borders of Canada ? Surely the hon. gentleman is not so narrow as that. But, what do these hon. gentlemen mean. I have listened to their speeches, but I fail to find out what their policy is. We are paying for immigrants from Germany. Does the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) condemn that ? I think that if the question is looked at fairly, hon. gentlemen will change their minds concerning it.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken of the rural delivery of mail. I do not think that we in Canada are ready to adopt that policy. I am inclined to think that it would be too expensive. We have too many other things to do. Our people are very anxious to have transportation facilities, ^they are in need of railways, public works, of canals-of many things that are more important to them than receiving their letters and newspapers at their own door. This appears to be the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, but it will be a very extravagant policy. They lecture us day after day on economy. But, if we introduce rural mail delivery, we must spend a great deal of money. It is estimated, I believe that it cost $30,000,000 in the United States. I do' not think it could be done for anything less in a sparsely settled country like Canada. At any rate it will cost a great deal of money-perhaps $20,000,000. I do not think we can afford to spend $20,000,000 in the carrying of our mails. Of course, like everybody else, I am proud of the record our post office has made. When the Liberals came into power, as everybody will remember, the post office service was in a very backward condition. Like all the other departments, it had become a kind of political machine. Mail contracts were giv-

en to favourites of the late government. When Sir William Mulock took charge of the post office as a member of this government, hon. gentlemen will remember there was a deficit of $781,000. One of the first acts he performed was to cancel a large number of improvident mail contracts-perhaps I should use a stronger term than ' improvident.' However, he cancelled them and put the contracts up to tender, the result being that he saved on these contracts the sum of $103,000 a year. If you consider that these contracts run for four years you will see that he saved no less than $412,000. It will be remembered, as it was drawn to the attention of the House this winter, that a proposition was laid before the late government to reduce the postage from 3 cents to 2 cents. But Sir Adolphe Caron, then Postmaster General, said it would be impossible to do so. Here are his words :
The government has no intention of reducing the rate of postage on letters. The loss of revenue would be $700,000.
It was only about three years after that that Sir Wm. Mulock took this step that was said to be impossible and made the reduction proposed. And we all know what the result was. He had deficits for the first two or three years and then he began to have surpluses. And if we look over the record for the last eleven years, every man must be proud of that record.
(1)	Postal facilities have been provided for the Yukon and for a large number of new settlements in the west at very great cost.
(2)	The number of letters increased from
116.028,000	in 1896 to 364,095,000 in 1907, an increase of 248,000,000. Of course there was also a large increase in the staff of the employees to handle all these letters.
(3)	The annual mileage or travel of the mail has Been increased by 12,254,211.
(4)	New post offices to the number of 2,186 Jmve been established.
(5)	7,941 money order and postal offices have been established.
(6)	298 new savings banks have been started.
(7)	The increase in the amount of money transmitted by money orders and postal notes aggregated the enormous sum of $34,847.440.
(8)	The number of savings bank depositors has doubled.
(9)	The salaries of postmasters of smaller places have been increased from $12 to $35, and, of course, in the larger post offices large additions to the service have been made and paid for. Notwithstanding all this, last year, instead of a deficit of $781,000 as in 1896, we had a surplus of $1,011,965 for nine months. Estimating at the rate for the whole year, we should have a surplus of $1,349,030 But. to make a comparison, with 1896, we should

add the old deficit, and this gives us a financial betterment of no less than $2,130,172. But even that is not all. By the reduction of the English postage from 5 cents to 2 cents, and the Canadian postage from 3 cents to 2 cents, we have saved another $1,000,000 which is in the pockets of the people of Canada. I say this is a record of which every Canadian ought to be proud, 1 do nbt care on which side or he ouse he is. There is one thing I want to suggest and I am glad that the Postmaster General (Mr. Leinieux) is here, and that is that the surplus should be spent in improving the system. We cannot afford rural delivery of mails, but we can afford a great many more daily mails than we have at present.
Speaking for my own province, and in looking over the post office returns there are 96 post offices in the province of Nova Scotia that have only a weekly service. Now in this 20th century I think there should be no people in this country receiving a mail only once a week. There are a good many who receive only two mails a week, and a good many others who receive only three mails. As much as possible I think we ought to give to the people in the country districts a better mail service. My idea would be to spend the whole of the surplus in improving the service, in increasing the number of daily mails. That would be doing the greatest good to the greatest number. Our farmers and farmers' sons would be more content to live on the land if they were brought into closer touch with civilization by getting a mail every day. I trust therefore that the Postmaster General will take that matter into consideration, and that instead of piling up surpluses he will, as the member for North Toronto says, ' open the floodgates,' atnd let us have a larger number of daily mails throughout the country.
I am open to conviction.

While I am talking about the financial state of the country, I wish to refer to the fact that the Intercolonial has shown such a good year, I would not be properly representing the people of Nova Scotia if I did not show an interest in the success of that great railway. That Intercolonial Railway, like the post office during the time of the Conservative regime was also a political machine. In 1896 it had been allowed to depreciate, the rails were worn out the roadbed was bad, the rolling stock was bad, it was a second-class affair all round. It had no western terminus, it ended in a field opposite the city of Quebec. It could not be expected to get business. But this government pushed it forward to the great city of Montreal, to the centre of commercial life in this country, and they did it against the determined opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite. Hon. gentlemen oppo-

site opposed that project, as they opposed every other progressive movement we have in this country for the last eleven years. They were not only opposed to that railway, hut they were opposed to the railway through the Crow's Nest Pass, which has done a great deal for the development of the west. They wrere opposed to the Grand Trunk Pacific, which lias broadened the habitable belt of this countrv and opened up an enormous district in the west. Nearly everybody in Canada is in favour of the Grand Trunk Pacific to-day. But the record of these gentlemen is that they were not only opposed to the Intercolonial coming to Montreal, but they have been opposed to every progressive movement to improve transportation which has been made by this government for the last eleven years. Now I was pointing out that this road had no western terminus. But this government provided one, the old 56-pound rails were taken up and replaced by 80 pound rails; better roadbed was made, new rolling stock was obtained, fine large engines were purchased, bridges were made and strengthened and built of steel, and we have now a splendid railway running down through the maritime provinces. We have some of the best trains you will find on the American continent : I do not think there is a better train .anywhere on this continent than the Maritime Express. Not only in the passenger service but in every service a great improvement has been made. Under the old system that existed in those lonesome eighteen years that we all deplore, when you shipped freight on board the Intercolonial you did not know when it would reach Montreal. Sometimes it was for weeks on the way. At present, we have a schedule train called the fast freight, that leaves Halifax and Sidney at a certain hour in the day, and arrives in Montreal under schedule time. It takes about 60 hours I think from Halifax to Montreal. But you are sure when you put your freight aboard that train that it will reach its destination in failtime. That train has done a great deal for the development of the industries of Eastern Canada; it has done a great deal for the fishing industry, because we are now certain that when we put a crate of fresh fish on board that train it will get through in proper time, whereas we could not be certain under the old system. Improvements of that kind have been made, and the Intercolonial to-day is a credit to the people of Canada.
But the Intercolonial is not perfect any more than the post office, and I have this criticism to make, that it has not done enough to develop traffic and to reach the outlying districts along the route, that it has not done enough to work up traffic by acquiring branch lines, and by building branch lines to places where traffic can be secured. The Intercolonial is a great artery passing through the country but has no veins to feed
it. No government that has existed so far have adopted the policy of building branch lines. You would scarcely believe it, that in the province of Nova Scotia, one of the oldest provinces in Canada, there is a district lying east of the city of Halifax, about 150 miles in length and forty miles in width, with about 40,000 of a population, with great resources of timber, a good agricultural country, a mining country, with large fishing resources, and that for thirty years this Intercolonial Railway has been skirting the northern border of that district, and I do not think they have ever sent an engineer into that district to explore it, and to see if it were possible to work up a traffic by building a branch into it. That was the policy of the Intercolonial under the past government and so far it is the policy under this government. So far we have not squarely faced the question of building branch lines. I trust that we will, I know that everything cannot be done at once. My hon. friends opposite are on the wrong side of that question also; because a few days ago my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who is the railway authority that hon. gentlemen opposite follow, said that the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial must stop. Now, Sir, I presume that is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, that they are following their leader in that as in other matters, and that if they were in power they would not spend another dollar on capital expenditure for the Intercolonial Railway. That means that we can never acquire any of the existing branch lines, that we can never build branch lines, for we cannot build them out of ordinary revenue as everybody knows. That seems to be the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, and is the same kind of policy that I have described in regard to the other railway and transportation proposals in this country. They are on the wrong side of that question as they have been on the wrong side of all the other progressive movements that have been made. I trust, however, that the government will take that matter up, that they will look at it carefully, and see where there are places that traffic could be worked up and where branch lines could properly and successfully be built, so that they may make of the Intercolonial, not only in name but in reality, the road of the people of Canada.
My hon. friends opposite have been condemning us for the expenditure. Now, Sir, it is true that we have spent a good deal of money during the the past eleven years. That question has been settled by the people on two or three different occasions. You will remember, Sir, that in the election of 1900 we -were condemned for this expenditure and we were returned by a very large majority when the people had pronounced their verdict. In the election of 1904 hon. gentlemen opposite, with the defeated candidates, who are so numerous among their friends, spoke in every hall and school house

and from every platform in Canada condemning this government for their large expenditure, but when the people marked their ballots you know what the verdict was. My judgment is that the people want expenditure, that they are anxious to have it and hon. gentlemen opposite, with the propositions they make from day to day, such as rural mail delivery, the building of tunnels and the building of this and that, although they condemn the government for doing these things, in their moments of weakness they seem to be in favour of large expenditure themselves. At all events, they have voted for most of these expenditures and they are now condemning the government for them. Not only are the people satisfied with these expenditures, but they are proud of the fact that this government has been able to expend so much money without putting the country in debt. The people are very much impressed with the fact that while the government have spent a large amount of money on capital account they have been able to do this out of ordinary revenue.
The Grand Trunk Pacific, for instance.

As my hon. friend has reminded me of the Grand Trunk Pacific, I would like to speak of that for a moment. We are proposing to spend this year $30,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific. We are proposing to borrow only $12,000,000 of that amount. Do my hon. friends think that is a very bad record? When we went into the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific we expected to borrow the whole of the money. We were not aware that we wovdd have a surplus with which to build any part of the road, but instead of borrowing this money we are going to be able to build a large portion of this road out of ordinary revenue. We are going to be able to invest $18,000,000 out of the ordinary revenue of the country in a permanent investment-not a debt at all- but an investment of our money that will bring the people 3 per cent for all time to come. Are my hon. friends not satisfied with that? Three per cent on $18,000,000 will bring over $500,000. We are making an investment that will put half a million dollars each year into the treasury of Canada for all time to come. When the youngest man opposite has reached his hundredth year, if he lives to be a hundred, the sum of half a million dollars will be paid into the treasury of Canada for the ordinary revenue of the country on account of the investment that we are making this year. Surely they ought to be satisfied with an expenditure of $30,000,000 and a borrowing of only $12,000,000. Yet they cry out about the terrible thing that we are doing. We expect to have a fair return from that investment, not only a return in interest, but a larger return in the development of the country. I am surprised that hon. gentle-Mr. SINCLAIR.
men do not get converted on that question. I could say a good deal, if I had the time, about the question of expenditure. I could point out that certain services of the country were very much neglected in the time of hon. gentlemen opposite, for example, public works on the coast of Nova Scotia. There was very little attention paid to that class of expenditures in the time of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) laid down the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to that question wrhen he said that these little places on the coast of Nova Scotia should not receive any consideration at the hands of the government, but that we ought to expend our money in the larger places, in the big places like Toronto. Those were the places where the Dominion government ought to spend their money and they should allow the people who live in the little places to go without such public works, or construct them at their own expense.
I would like to ask my hon. friend when and where the hon. member for North Toronto ever said that?

In a speech on the 6th day of July, 1905, which my hon. friend will find in ' Hansard,' page 8926. The hon. member for North Toronto, in discussing these expenditures, said:
I never knew that it would be possible to find in the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, the names of so many places where wharfs and breakwaters and piers could possibly be built, as I find in the estimate which has been placed before us this year. All geography needs to be revised, all knowledge by the most liberal-minded and best travelled has to be extended in order to grasp the almost infinite number of little places in the province of Nova Scotia where large expenditures are made, and I am bound to say, out of nine-tenths of which no corresponding revenue at all comes to this country.
Then, a little further on he makes this statement:	.
The expenditure is going up millions and millions every year, this government usurping enterprises which ought to be carried out by individuals, by corporations, by municipalities and by provinces. It is a nice thing for the provinces, but it is a demoralizing thing to the countrv as a whole.
It does not bear out the statement that the hon. gentleman made.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it does.
Absolutely, no. There Is not a word about Toronto in connection with it.	[DOT]

My hon. friend was talking about the construction of wrharfs and public works on the coast of Nova Scotia and he made the statement in effect that the government should not undertake these works at all in the little places, but that they should be built by the munici-

palities and provinces, meaning that if the fishermen in these places along the coast of Nova Scotia wanted public wharfs or breakwaters built, they must tax themselves for them, while the larger places like the city of Toronto are to get all the money that is to be spent for public works by this government. While the hon. gentleman was condemning the expenditure on the coast of Nova Scotia there was before the House at that very time a very large expenditure for a public work in the city of Toronto and he did not raise his voice against it. That was allowed to go through ; but if it is proposed to build a little wharf for the protection of fishermen and for the use of the fishing industry on the coast of Nova Scotia he condemns it. What does he mean, when he refers to an infinite number of little places ? Does he mean that those little places should have these wharfs or does he mean that they should not have them ? I think if the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler) will analyze that speech of his leader from North Toronto, he will find that he is opposed to these expenditures for wharfs and breakwaters on the coast of his own province as well as on the coast of Nova Scotia. That seems to be the policy of the hon. gentlemen opposite, but it is not the policy that will be acceptable to the people of the country. The people of Canada are prepared to develop not only the west but the older provinces as well. We have a good country in the east, we are doing to-day everything in our power to develop the industries and the resources that we have in the east as well as in the west, and if hon. gentlemen opposite would take an enlightened view of this question, if they would look at it as we look at it on this side, they would support us in these expenditures instead of condemning us year after year. I could continue this argument at greater length if the hon. gentleman desires me to do so, but I think I have satisfied him that his party have been on the wrong side of this question, as they have been on the wrong side of the transportation question.
On the wrong side of the House.

This shows that when my hon. friend was a minister he spent nearly as much in public works in that one city as he did for wharfs, breakwaters and improvements on the whole coast of Nova Scotia. It will be noticed in this list that the large expenditures are in 1887 and 1891. Perhaps my hon. friend from Hamilton will know why the expenditures in Nova Scotia were so large in those particular years ? Perhaps he will tell us ? What does that mean ? My hon. friend is always very fond of percentages, and it is an extraordinary circumstance that in the year of the election 1S87, he should have increased the expenditure on the coast of Nova Scotia by 1,500 per cent compared with what it was two years before. This is the hon. gentleman who lectures us, who day after day turns up the whites of his eyes and lectures the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance on buying the people of Canada with their own money. I could hardly believe that when he was Minister of Finance ' he would open the flood gates in that way during the election years. Surely it was not done in the public interest ? He is always asking if these expenditures by this government were made in the public interest. Was it in the public interest to increase the expenditure by 1,500 per cent in the year of the election, or was it done in a moment of weakness ?
Would the hon. member point to any expenditure made at that time which was not in the public interest ?
Certainly not. I think they were in the public interest; the trouble was there were not enough of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there had not been an occasional election we would never have got anything.

Even the election in the county I represent did not bring any money because we had a habit of sending members here to support the Liberal opposition and during fourteen out of the eighteen years there was no money at all spent in my county. Expenditures were made in certain other portions of Nova Scotia ; lighthouses, breakwaters and improvements of that kind were required in Guysborough but no expenditures were made although eloquent appeals were made by Mr. Fraser and Mr. Kirk, my predecessors. No money was granted and we were told by a minister of the Crown who .visited us on one occasion that if we wanted any money we must vote for the government. We were told very plainly by a late Minister of Public Works that that was the only way we could get any money for expenditures in Guysborough. But we chose to support the Liberal opposition and continued to do so during the whole period. We are there still at the old stand, and will continue to support the same party in the next election.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends are cheering. I tell them it is a fact, that it would be very difficult to return even one Conservative in Nova Scotia if the elections were to come on now. The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) looks a little alarmed at that, but I think that even the people of Colchester will be of the same oninion as ourselves and will say that the present government is good enough for Nova Scotia.

New Brunswick is down in the east.
Motion agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday ?
